speechtext: ['While I do not pretend to talk about railway matters, I must call the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to an incident that occurred in the county of Peel when I was a member of the county council. An electric railway company came to the county council and asked for liberty to run its track along a certain part of the highway, but the council flatly refused because it was thought that accidents would result to farmers with their horses and cattle on the highway if street cars were allowed to be run there. The county council took the view that if the electric railway were a paying affair the promoters should be compelled to buy their right of way the same as any other railway company. * It is very annoying to farmers, particularly with young horses, to go out on the highway and meet an electric railway ear. I think that the rights of rural municipalities should be recognized in this matter as well as those of cities. If an electric railway is a paying enterprise the company should be compelled to buy their right of way in the direction which they wish to go. The county of Peel absolutely refused to grant this company running rights over a certain road from Toronto to Oakville. I know that in our section of the country the people are opposed to allowing electric railways to be established on the highways, because of the difficulty they have with young horses. Street ears can be controlled on the road and no damage will be done to them, but if their operation on the highways is legalized by legislation they have a right to run Mr. HENDERSON.\nthere and in the event of damage being done to people in vehicles drawn by horses which are not manageable, the injured parties have no redress. I think the rights of municipalities should be guarded as well as those of cities and towns.\nProgress reported.']

On section 59-paid up stock may be issued for certain purposes.

We adopted the section referring to paid up stock as it is in the existing law. My first inclination was to make it more effective, and to, if possible, require additional precautions and safe guards, but upon more mature consideration I would not make any very strenuous effort to retain the clause in the Bill if it is the wish of the committee to strike it out. If it were eliminated from the Bill I do not see that any great inconvenience would arise, I am not going to move, however, that it be struck out, unless hon. gentlemen who have considered the matter deem it advisable to do so. Under the existing law the board of directors have the power, and if we preserve it at all I think we should put that

power into the hands of the company. 1 would suggest the following as an alternative :
The company may make and issue as paid up stock, shares in the company whether subscribed or not, and may allot and hand over in payment tor plant, rolling stock, docks, elevators, wharfs, warehouses or materials of any kind, and also for the services of contractors and engineers, such an amount of such stock as shall be the fair and bona fide value for the property purchased or services rendered as aforesaid; not being promotion services ; due regard being had for the fair value of the stock, and such issue and allotment of stock shall be binding on the company and such stock shall not be assessable for calls.

speechtext: I would like to ask the minister whether that clause would not enable a person to act as a contractor in disposing of the bonds of the company, and to obtain from the company for his services a certain amount of paid up stock on which he would not pay a dollar ? I think the amendment is open to the same objection that was referred to before in the discussion on the original clause, that persons with financial influence who might be employed to place a large amount of bonds or debentures, might get practical control of the company without putting a dollar into it.

I think what the hon. gentleman suggests, and a great many other things as well, could be done under this clause. I do not think it would be possible to frame a clause that would not be liable to abuse.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think the section as now proposed is just as objectionable as the old clause. The word ' contractor ' in the old clause was generally supposed to refer to a contractor who undertook to construct a railway; but I think that these contractors in reality do not often have stock given to them. It is more generally given to financial contractors, and all the objections raised against this method of disposing of the stock of the company without cash being paid for it apply to this clause quite as much as they did to the old clause. I see no objection to issuing stock for the payment of right of way or equipment, because in such cases it is given for a property which has a specific value; but the value of the services of a gentleman who has influence on the money market in placing bonds is an absolutely unknown quantity, and the company could give to such a person as much stock as it chose, and there would be no possible check upon it. What is the need of putting the word ' contractor ' in this clause at all ? If it were useful for a company to pay for its right of way or its rolling stock or anything else with stock, it could do so; but when you put in a word which would enable the company to give stock to the kind of contractor I have referred to, you throw the whole thing open without any possibility of a check upon the company.

My hon. friend's objection is chiefly to the use of the word ' contractor.' That word has been in this section ever since the first enactment, so far as I know, and I question very much whether it is subject to such a wide interpretation as he supposes, or that it would be held to mean more than a person who contracted with the company for construction or for some other work on the line. I question very much whether it would be held to apply to a person who acted as a broker for the sale of bonds. If it did, I do not imagine that it would be any more objectionable than it would be as applied in the other cases. If the company has bonds to disjtose of, it has to pay brokers or bankers or other financial men to dispose of them; and if the stock had a fixed value, I am quite sure that the company would not be willing to pay any more than what the ordinary percentage on a business basis would amount to. If they had not any value in the market, it would be pretty difficult to say what limit might be put upon the issue of such shares. I think the section is some improvement on the existing law, but I do not say that it would not be liable to great abuse, and if the hon. gentleman wishes to move to strike it out altogether, I would not raise any objection.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think the section is of no real value except to enable the company to issue stock without getting any money for it, and it is important that the company should not be allowed to issue a very large amount of capital. I would therefore move that this clause be struck out.

sale of any such forfeited shares be more thin sufficient to pay all arrears of calls and interest thereon due at the time of such sale and the expenses attending the declaration of forfeiture and sale thereof, the surplus shall, on demand, be paid to the defaulter.

speechtext: The bon. gentleman will observe that under subsection 5 it is necessary that the handwriting of the Secretary of State and the Deputy Registrar General shall be proved. That might be rather inconvenient. In the Canada Evidence Act, according to my recollection of it, the signatures of officers of state are not required to be proved. speechtext: I would like to point out to the hon. minister, before the amendment is adopted, that by striking out subsection 3 he leave* out the provision requiring the mortgage to be deposited with the Secretary of State, and providing that until so deposited and until notice is given no such mortgage shall have any force or effect. Does the hon. minister designedly leave that out ?
Yes, I think it is a very objectionable clause. In subsection 4, as we propose to amend the section, provision is made for the publication of notice in the ' Canada Gazette.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
My point is that if some penalty is not put upon them they may
never deposit the mortgage, and yet the mortgage is in force. The object' of the other subsection was to compel them to deposit it. Now, they are not bound to register it, and it is only made directory that they shall deposit it where anybody can find it. It is in force the instant it is executed, and unless it is made obligatory to deposit it the mortgage is in force and it is impossible for the public to get at It. In Ontario we always register these mortgages in a land office, and they are always registered unless a special clause relieves the company from the necessity. I rose to mention the fact that the mortgage becomes in force now the instant it is executed and there is nothing to compel the company to deposit it.
Subsection 4 provides in explicit terms that the mortgage shall be deposited. It is not required to be registered under the provisions of the ordinary Registration Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it not desirable that there should be some means by which the public can have knowledge of what property is covered by a conveyance of this kind ? Of course, there is a provision in subsection 4 of section 112 that the document shall be deposited in the office of the Secretary of State.
That is in lieu of the ordinary registration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, but the difficulty is that you do not insert the usual provisions of the Registration Act which require the conveyance, or deed, or mortgage, to be registered, and in default of registration make it void as against the conveyance of any person who shall first register the same. While there is a direction to deposit this mortgage in the office of the Se'cretary of State, there seems to be no result whatever in case the document is not so deposited. It is a provision which the railway company could ignore absolutely, in whica case there would be no way of getting access to the document. It might be important that the public should know to what extent a railway company has mortgaged its undertakings. People who are doing business with the railway company would want to know that. The hon. gentleman has made a change in that respect from the former law. Has he given any consideration to the possible results which I have just mentioned ?

There is no doubt the other clause was distinctly put, was a penalty if the mortgage was not deposited:
Until so deposited and notice given no such mortgage shall have any force or effect.
The notice would not be so important, but it would leave an unprecedented position in a legal sense. I quite agree that it is not necessary to record it elsewhere than in the office of the Secretary of State, but to leave

it directory, so that if the company see fit they may not do it, and the mortgage will go into force the moment it is executed, I think is objectionable. I do not see any hardship in the old law requiring that they shall deposit it.

The old law did not say that. That is the provision of the Bill as we introduced it, but these words are not in the existing law at all. Upon the first consideration w'e gave the subject it struck us, as it would strike any lawyer, that perhaps that provision had better go in, but it does not seem to be wise to continue it. That is the view we arrived at. Mortgage deeds and other conveyances have not been habitually or largely registered in registration Offices throughout the country. Whatever is done with them in a public way is simply to deposit the mortgage, according to the provisions of the existing law, in the office of the Secretary of State.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The practice in the different provinces has probably been different. At one time in the province of Nova Scotia these documents were required to be registered, but the law was so amended providing that they need not be registered or filed. I understand from my hon. friend from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) that the practice has been to register them in Ontario. The only circumstance I want to bring to the hon. minister's attention is that it seems to me that in some way or other the public have the right to inform themselves of the contents of these documents, and you could hardly accomplish that result by a provision of this kind.
You might put a peualty in.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You might put in a penalty for every day's delay after the document had been executed.
Two months is the limit under the existing law. We might make it less than that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
There is a further provision here that it shall not be necessary to register under any provincial law. If you want to build the real estate in Ontario you must register the mortgage, and I do not think you will find any mortgage upon which bonds are founded in Ontario but what is registered in every county through which the line passes. I know I have had to register several and that was the custom of the Grand Trunk Railway. In Ontario they did that at that time, and I am not sure but that there was a special clause in the Railway Act, or in a special Act, making the bonds a lien on all the property of the railway company without registration or formal conveyance. You have removed here the necessity for regis-Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
tering them locally, and I would like the minister to give his consideration to that matter.
We propose to substitute this deposit in the office of the Secretary of State in lieu of registration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think you will find an express provision in the Registry Act of Ontario, for instance, which makes it necessary that mortgages should be registered. I presume the mortgagee would desire to have the registration for his own protection.

speechtext: I move to insert after the words ' But the board shall not grant leave to any company,' the words ' incorporated after the passing of this Act.'

speechtext: The difficulty about this amendment seems to be that so far as all existing railways are concerned it authorizes the board, without the consent of the municipality, to grant permission for the construction of a tramway or street railway along the streets of any municipality. That is a very important amendment, for it practically repeals the clause wrhich was agreed upon the other day. I should think the minister ought to state to the committee the reasons which induced him to make so important a change.

Since the clause was introduced one or two of the companies have complained that we were taking away from them specific rights which they had acquired, and the taking away of which w-ould have a very injurious effect on their interests, financial and otlienvise. The securities they were arranging to finance would be seriously prejudiced, and we would practically bar any further extension of the rights on which their undertaking had been started. I confess that the words we have put into the hands of the chairman would free all existing companies from the restriction imposed by the clause.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It would destroy the value of the clause.

It is a very serious question ns to how we could deal with a case of this kind. For example, here is a company which is in operation, and which lias acquired its status, iinancial and otherwise, on the strength of the lines it has already built and other lines which it has in contemplation. If we enabled a civic corporation to bowl them out entirely without any possibility of relief from any quarter, we would be pursuing a rather hazardous course with respect to such an undertaking. We can imagine the case of a couple of rival corporations operating in one city, one of them being very much more influential than the other, and being able to impose its will, as it were, upon the municipal body, and inducing it to refuse to allow the other corporation to make its extensions, while allowing the rival corporation to make all the extensions it desired. It would seem unfair that such distinctions should exist, and that the arbitrary power should rest with the municipal body to favour the one corporation and refuse to extend equal privileges to the other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Could not that condition of affairs obtain with regard to companies hereafter incorporated ?

It might ; but when parliament is granting these incorporations, it would no doubt be put in possession by the promoters of all the necessary facts and circumstances, so that it could govern itself accordingly. But it looks to me as though, while we were moving in a direction which would meet with the acceptance of the public in the majority of cases, such legislation might and doubtless would work very injuriously as respects others. It might cover one ground without covering the other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the minister lay on the Table the memoranda of protests which he has received with respect to this clause as amended ?
I have been called on personally.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Might not provision be made for those specific cases instead of amending the clause so as to destroy its value ? Around every city and town in Canada at the present these tram railways have their lines, and if this clause is amended as proposed, it will practically destroy all the advantages which the minister was good enough to give us the other day.
I do not understand that. '
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The minister can readily see that if this clause is amended as proposed. it leaves it wide-open to the commission to allow any railway to run through the streets of cities whether the corporation 191
is willing or not. The amendment he proposes is simply deplorable.

On the same line I wish to point out that the city of Toronto receives an immense and growing revenue from its street railway franchise. The revenue will disappear entirely unless the streets of the city are protected from the aggression of the railway companies. They will have lines of their own independent of the municipality. In that way you would take away the great revenue which the city has at present from that source. Toronto receives a quarter of a million dollars a year from its street railway franchise. If the railways could come into the city under this law, the cohtrol of the street railway franchise would be taken away from the city.

I do not think that would follow at all. I can mention to the committee one case which has been very much before my mind, and which has been dealt with by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council on several cases ; that is, the case of the Montreal Terminal Company. This company had occasion to make application to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council from time to time, to be allowed to make extensions under their charter through different streets of the city of Montreal, and the way the matter has worked out has been this. The committee has always recognized that the city authorities must be consulted, and there has been no instance in which it has been necessary for the committee to make an order adverse to the city council. But the city council had not the arbitrary power to exclude corporations from the use of the streets without the approval of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. I may say, as a matter of fact, what is pretty well known in the city, that the Montreal Street Railway Company is very much opposed to the terminal company having these rights, and it is a very influential corporation, and has exercised its influence as against this company; and if the Railway Committee had not been supreme in the matter, the terminal company would probably have been refused the privilege which was given to the other company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does not the operation of its lines in the city of Montreal depend on the good will of the city council ?
It does, although its charter does not say so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
If this amendment carries will not the position of the city of Montreal be seriously jeopardized ? The contract 'o,f the Terminal Railway Company operating in the city has several years to run, and at the end of that time the council may renew



the contract or not as it pleases. I have a memorandum here respecting the Montreal Terminal Railway.
It is not subject to the consent of the council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I understand that the city has the right to designate the streets through which the company shall run, the number of years it shall run, and the conditions generally under which the road shall be operated. I would not be a party to the company being deprived of any of its rights, but I do not want to see the municipality deprived of any of its rights or privileges. My hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) has pointed out the serious effects this amendment would have upon the city of Toronto. With all due respect to the members who may compose the railway board, we would greatly prefer being allowed to manage our own streets and our own interests without the interference of any board or tram car company. The interests of a quarter of a million of people ought to be of greater moment to parliament than the carrying out of the schemes of two or three railway promoters. 'The franchise of the Toronto Street Railway Company will in ten or twelve years be worth twenty millions of dollars to the city of Toronto. That city, which has the exclusive right to operate street cars on its own streets, has given that right to the Toronto Street Railway Company for thirty years, nearly one-half of which term has expired. That city has the best tram car system in Christendom, and should be allowed to continue in control of its own affairs. The company should be made to come to the city ; but the hon. gentleman, by his amendment, would take away our control and say to the promoters of railway companies :	If you can get the ear
of the railway commissioners you may go into Montreal or Hamilton or Toronto, or any other city, whether the corporation likes it or not. Such a provision would work a monstrous injustice to the municipalities. The interests of the people in our great municipalities ought to come in front of the interests of these promoters. The citizens of every large municipality are desirous of getting the most perfect tram car system they can, and the franchises given by this parliament would not be worth the paper they are written on were it not for the large aggregations of human beings in the cities into which these tramways enter. If the municipalities impose conditions upon the companies, it is the people who have to pay. The promoters do not put then1 hands into their pockets and pay out whatever sum may be charged by the municipalities for the use of their streets. The regulation of the traffic, the conditions under which cars are allowed on the streets, the number of cars, the

fares, the protection to life and limb-every one of these should be provided for by the municipal authorities, and I would ask my hon. friend, who has put his hand to the plough and given us a reasonable measure of protection from the charter mongers, not to take away what he gave us a week or two ago, and what we accepted ns a generous measure of protection. If the position of the Terminal Railway in Montreal be jeopardized, if its rights be prejudiced by this clause, let special provision be made for that railway. No municipality desires to take away any right it has given. What we stenuousiy object to are these insidious attempts made by promoters to get greater privileges over the streets of municipalities.

My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) speaks about a reasonable measure of protection by the amendment given to the municipalities. The hon. minister will remember that I did not agree that that was reasonable, because it only applies to cities and towns and left out townships and villages. In my opinion, townships and villages have as much right to be protected as cities and towns. Of course I am in favour of justice being done to the cities and towns, but I also want our country districts and villages to be protected. Take the Hamilton and Grimsby Electric Railway, which runs through the counties of Wentworth and Lincoln upon the only highway between the escarpment and the lake from the city of Hamilton through Grimsby to Vineland, some twenty-five miles, of which escarpment the mountain at Hamilton and the Heights of Queens-ton are the principal elevations, and which is the only road that runs between these points on account of the irregular width of space of land between the escarpment and the lake. Certain conditions were imposed upon that road by the municipalities when allowing the railway to go on the highway, but if this amendment carries, this railway board can interefere with these restrictions and break the by-laws and conditions imposed by the municipalities upon this company. The board may say that it is in the interests of Canada that that railway should use steam or be relieved from certain regulations imposed upon it by the municipalities. tinder the Electric Railway Act, which is an Ontario statute, and under which this railway company is incorporated, this railway could not run a foot without the consent of the municipalities, as I showed by the statute I quoted a week or two ago. This railway connects with the Canadian Pacific Railway for freight and traffic and gets its charter from the Ontario legislature. Under that charter, it could not run a foot on any highway in either of those counties, as I pointed out to the hon. minister the other day, without the consent of

the municipalities. It had to make its bargain with these municipalities, and are not these municipalities the parties most competent to look after their own interests ? They are not innocent babes or people of unsound mind who require to have their interests managed by executors or curators or guardians. The reeves and councillors of the townships, the mayors and aldermen of the towns, are just as well able, yes, much more able to look after the municipal interests and use of highways than this railway board. But if this amendment passes, the bargains which the municipalities made with the railway companies may be set aside, and the railway board is to control the highways instead of the municipalities who are responsible for the repair and safety of the highways. If this passes, what would be the result ? This board, if it thinks fit can say of the bargains made by the railway companies with the municipalities that they are improvident and unreasonable and so set aside all these bargains. In other words, it allows the railway to use and to sell to Somebody else something to which they have no right and which they have contracted not to use except under certain conditions and limitations. This would remove restrictions imposed by municipalities and hand over control to the board. The highways are properly under the control of the municipalities ; and surely the people who elect the reeves and councillors, and who have the opportunity once a year to declare by tbeir votes whether they are satisfied with the acts of their representatives or not, and who are most intimately concerned with the proper use of these highways, should be allowed to control the use of those highways. This proposal of the minister still leaves the villages and townships out in the cold. But, while I think that the townships and villages should be protected, as an honest man, I am bound to say that the towns and cities should be protected also. The hon. minister proposes to restrict this to railways that are not now incorporated. This is equivalent to saying to me : I will allow you to possess a fortune five years from now if you can get it in the meantime, but what property you have to-day I will take away from you. These railways are now existing and are running under certain limitations, and the hon. minister says that only new railways shall be compelled to come under the control of the municipalities. The municipalities have made bargains with these railway companies, but these bargains will go by the board if this proposal is adopted.
There is nothing to be gained by making exaggerated statements concerning what we are dealing with here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Mine are not exaggerated statements.
191i

They are most extremely exaggerated statements. No one proposes to interfere with the powers of the municiapli-ties to impose whatever terms they choose to impose. All that the board does is to say, that one street and not another shall be used. That class of questions arises in respect of these tramways under the existing law. Take, for instance, the case of the Montreal Terminal. Their charter gives them the right to use the streets of the city, but it does not give them the right to go upon the streets for the purpose of laying down tracks or otherwise using them until the corporation has looked the question over and has decided whether this street or some other street is the one they should have the power to use, or until they have decided whether they will require such a percentage or contribution from the earnings of the company, or what other regulation they shall deem it in the interest of the public to impose. That is the state of the law as it is to-day, and it is absurd to say that if this amendment were passed it would cut that ground away. It would not do so. All that it would do would be to give to the board of railway commissioners powers which the Railway Committee of the Privy Council now possess to enable them to say whether or not the absolute refusal to allow the company to make any use of any of the streets is a refusal which is a just, proper and reasonable one on the part of the municipal corporation. That is all that this Bill proposes. The Railway Committee of the Privy Council, as I say, has that power to-day, and I want to say that in no single instance has that tribunal made any order which was not made ultimately and finally, with the consent of the city corporation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But this board may do so.

This board would exercise their jurisdiction, I apprehend, in the same way as the Railway Committee of the Privy Council has exercised its jurisdiction. Tnere is no reason to suppose otherwise. Now, my hon. friend could not expect that oue who is not closely associated, either as a citizen or otherwise with the city of Toronto could appreciate the superlative importance and grandeur of that city. We who reside at a distance cannot grasp the infinity of those great qualities which these hon. gentlemen's town possesses, and we can only gaze upon it from afar in wonder and admiration. My hon. friend may discover in that circumstance some little explanation why we cannot see the force- at least I am unable to see the force-of much that he suggests. Very much that my hon. friend has said that would apply to the common towns of the country, such as Montreal, Hamilton, London, Halifax and

St. John, I can fully agree with. I think that these ordinary towns ought to have a great deal to say with respect to the use of their own streets. I might, perhaps, if I knew Toronto, be prepared to admit that, as respects the streets of that great city, the corporation ought to have everything to say-and more. But, for the reason I have stated, I cannot go further than would be applicable to the ordinary towns of the country. Now, with regard to the ordinary towns, authority has been given to companies to lay down their tracks in the streets. At the same time, parliament in giving that power said that that power should be exercised subject to the control and direction of the corporation of the city. Now, the company in Montreal to which I referred, under general legislation was given that power. But the city corporation may make it a condition of the use of a particular street that a portion of the revenues of the company shall be given to the city. These revenues might never attain the magnitude of those in the city of Toronto, but still, they might reach a very respectable sum. Parliament has given these powers, and it has been represented to me that this parliament, having given these privileges, ought not arbitrarily to take them away. If that argument is one which ought to have any weight at all, I am sure the company will join with me in endeavouring to work out the problem of the recognition of these privileges consistently with the maintenance of proper rights on the part of the city corporations.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
With regard to the proposed .further amendment to section 184, I wish to call the attention of the minister to the fact that this is not merely a question of rivalry between two companies in a municipality, but rather a question between any one company and the municipality itself. I refer to that particularly, because the city of Hamilton, which I represent, is very materially interested in this matter, not because of any rivalry or competition between two railway companies, but because of its own position should the Board of Railway Commissioners see fit, under any power secured here, to grant powers to railway companies to pass through the streets of a city. There is in Hamilton a street railway company enjoying rights granted by the city itself, not by any parliament or legislature. The legislature incorporated the company with certain powers, but the city of Hamilton, like many other municipalities, had the absolute power to define what streets the company should construct its works upon, and all the accompanying con-Hon. Mr. BLAIR.	.	[DOT] *! ,
ditions, rates and terms, just as if it were the parliament itself. Under those conditions the city of Hamilton has granted power to the street railway company there for a limited number of years. The hon. gentleman must see that the power that is proposed to be given to the Board of Railway Commissioners under the General Railway Act, is not a limited power for a perpetual power. Now the city may say. we are willing to grant privileges to a railway company for ten, fifteen, twenty or thirty years ; but the Board of Railway Commissioners are not bound by the wishes or the opinions of the city in that regard. Under present conditions, it is, I think, the intention of almost all the municipalities in this country where street railways have an existence, to take over these railways and operate them at the expiration of the present charters. Now, if in ten or fifteen years hence the corporation of the city of Hamilton, for instance, should think it to the interest of the people to run the street car service itself, it is a most important feature of the whole thing whether another body, some other company, should have the power to compete with the corporation upon other of its streets, under power granted by the Board of Railway Commissioners, who know nothing whatever of the local wants or interests, who perhaps may live at Ottawa, and know as little about the city of Hamilton as they do of the city of Vancouver or the town of Moncton. I think it must be obvious to the committee that this 'parliament cannot well deal with any question about the operation of street railways in municipalities. The further amendment that is proposed to be out in this clause, as I understand it is one under which the board may allow privileges to street railway companies heretofore incorporated, and in spite of the opinion of the municipality concerned. That is the objection I take to it. Now with regard to the terminal railway in Montreal. I understand that a letter lias been sent by Mr. Mullarkey, secretary of that company, to the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). That is a company that does not possess any special privileges. Mr. Mullarkey says, quoting the language of the charter :
The company may lay out, construct, and operate branch or circuit lines, to be operated by electricity only, in such streets in the city of Montreal as are designated by the council of said city, and subject to such terms and conditions as are imposed upon the company by the said council.
This is a material point, because the council designates the streets upon which they may run, subject to such terms and conditions as are imposed upon the company by the city council. Now it does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, in face of a charter granted upon such conditions, to give to a Board of Railway Commissioners, who know as little

about the wants and interests of Montreal as I do, the power to Ignore the terms and conditions which the corporation of Montreal may wish to impose-I say that seems to me a monstrous stretching of the powers of this parliament. According to my view, this parliament has no more right* to deal with the question of street railways in the city of Montreal, or the city of Hamilton, than it has with the canals, if they exist, in Mars-they have nothing whatever to do with them. That is my judgment, and I think the government should be careful how they put into a General Railway Act any words that would appear to interfere with the independence, rights and legislative powers of the provinces. 'There can be no question that it was intended that the provinces should deal with nil such matters as these ; and I think it is a grave matter for this government to throw any doubt upon that power. But if there be any doubt, if the hon. gentleman wishes to reserve all the rights heretofore granted by parliament, if he thinks it desirable to protect what is called vested rights, I recommend the suggestion that is made here that the particular company that may be affected by this legislation should be specially mentioned. Although it may 'be said it is not a good form of legislation to mention in a General Railway Act a particular company, and its particular rights, I beg to call the hon. gentleman's attention to section 276, of the General Railway Act, of 1888 now in force, where a special condition with regard to two railway companies was provided for, because they had rights that perhaps other companies did not have. Section 276 puts certain restrictions and conditions upon all the railways of the country, but expressly reserves the rights, under certain charters, of two railway companies that are expressly mentioned in that section. Now if there is any question whatever as to the rights of this terminal company in Montreal, under the words which I presume are correctly quoted by the secretary of that company, if there be any question at all as to the propriety of reserving its rights, or assumed rights, the hon. gentleman should put in a restriction safeguarding whatever rights it may have under its charter. If, before this legislation came before the House, they had obtained from the city of Montreal any rights upon the streets of that city, those rights are now in existence, and surely it will be an easy matter to put in words to protect and preserve them. It ought not to be left a matter of doubt throughout the whole Dominion as to the rights of every city, town, or municipality, because some company in Montreal claims to have a peculiar right. The municipalities want to know where they stand, and if there is one exceptional case let that be mentioned in the clause, and not leave every municipality
in the whole Dominion in a state of uncertainty as to its position.
The MINISTER OF, RAILWAYS AND CANALS. I am not at all desirous that this committee should extend any favours to any of these electric railways operating inj any of the cities. All I desire, and in that I am at one with hon. gentlemen opposite, is that we shall not take away from any company that has had a particular franchise conferred upon it that franchise in whole or in part. I go the full length that my hon. friends opposite have gone as to the character of the legislation that ought to be passed by this parliament on that subject. I do not think we ought to be easily convinced that we should legislate upon this subject, and I agree that these companies ought to go to the provincial legislatures in the first place, and in the second place I am prepared to go as far as any hon. member of this committee in giving a full measure of control to the municipal councils of the different towns and cities. I am willing that they should have the right to say whether they will have a street railway at all. I do not lag behind hon. gentlemen opposite in respect to that branch of the question. Now, what I do desire, though, is that we should say all that is really necessary in order that we may leave these companies exactly as we find them.
We quite agree with that.

My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) has read one of the clauses of the charter of the Montreal Terminal Railway. I have no doubt it is correctly quoted by Mr. Mullarkey who claims that this company has the right to lay down its lines in the city of Montreal, of course, under the restrictions contained in the Act. All the Acts which have been passed by parliament in recent years have contained similar restrictions; that is to say that the terms and conditions under which these privileges shall be exercised shall be under the control of the municipality and that the council shall designate which of the streets shall be occupied. The charter does not say ' which, if any,' but ' which ' of the streets. When parliament, whether wisely or unwisely, gave to the company the right to run their street railway within the city upon the streets of the city, I take it that it would be a distinct violation, or a refusal to submit to the voice and direction of parliament, if the city should refuse to allow any of its streets to be occupied for that purpose. I take it that inference is clear and I believe my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Borden) will agree that it would be a disregard of an Act of parliament if any- city council or municipal body were to refuse to allow a company to get into the city at all. That is practically one of the conditions we are facing and in the

interpretation which the Railway Committee placed upon that Act we thought, that, while the city council of Montreal might properly impose all reasonable and proper conditions when designating the streets, they were bound to designate the streets or else the legislation would be absolutely nugatory and in that view, after having refused in the first place to name any streets, if my memory serves me, the city council were advised to agree and did agree. So that there was really no trouble and they came to an agreement with the company later on when they found what view was-entertained by the railway company and everything went on satisfactorily. If we were to put a provision in this Bill to the effect, that this clause should not deprive any company chartered by parliament of its rights to lay down its line, subject to proper oversight and direction and subject, to the conditions of the special Act, I think we would not be going too far as we would simply be preserving the rights which had beien created. But, I do not think we should limit it to this particular company. I do not know but that there may be a great many others and to specifically mention one particular company in the way which the bon. gentleman suggests is not legislation which one would wish to favour. True, it was done in 1888, but it is not a desirable system at all. I am sure my hon. friend would not think that it would be a desirable thing to do if it could be very safely avoided. If rights have been created by this parliament, can there be any reasonable objection to say that it is not proposed to take away these rights by this Bill ? I do not think, if a proper interpretation and construction are put upon the meaning of this Bill, that we are depriving the town or city council of the right of imposing terms. We are not doing that. The Railway Committee or the board of commissioners or any body constituted for the purpose of deciding these matters would be bound to consider what the special Act required, and would be bound to make their ruling in accordance with the spirit and letter of the Act creating the corporation. I do not think that there is any good ground for taking a serious view of the matter at all. I am perfectly willing to withdraw the words I was proposing to the committee and substituting anything else that might meet more fully the views of hon. gentlemen who are discussing this question if proper words can be chosen for that purpose.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the question is a broader one than has been put by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. We are to-day in the midst of a constitutional revolution in this country, and the party in power, by the legislation they have put through this House recently, are fast carrying this country into a, legislative union. The provinces are being stripped of many Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
of their powers and especially have we seen this session and during past sessions a general raiding of municipal rights particularly in the province of Ontario. If the municipal rights of the province of Ontario can be raided as they have been raided by this parliament, repeatedly, then the civil and religious rights of the other provinces will also be attacked and very soon we will find that the old battle of provincial rights will be up again. I take the position that wrongful legislation has been repeatedly passed through this House, legislation raiding the rights of the provinces, and to put the question which is now before the committee and before parliament, the question of the Toronto and Hamilton Railway, I propose to read to the committee the case of the municipalities against this raiding. This is well set out in a paper which I have in my hand and which says :
Memoranda re Bill 147, Incorporating the Toronto and Hamilton Railway Company.
This Bill contemplates the incorporation of an electric railway to run from Toronto to Hamilton, a whole distance of some forty miles. It authorizes amalgamation with or the acquisition by purchase, lease or otherwise, In whole or in part, of the franchises, works, plant and other property of the Hamilton Radial Electric Railway Company, the Hamilton. Grimsby and Beamsville Electric Railway Company. the Hamilton Street Railway Company, the Toronto and Mimico Railway Company, the Metropolitan Railway Company, and the Toronto Suburban Railway Company, all companies'Incorporated by the legislative assembly of the province of Ontario, and all subject to municipal consent, and control.
The purchase of the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto Railway Company, a company incorporated by the Dominion parliament but which has not yet been constructed, is also authorized.
The Bill also declares the undertaking to be ' a work for the general advantage of Canada,' and provides that upon the acquisition of any of the lines of any of the companies above enumerated that the Railway Act of Canada shall apply to such lines and ' to the maintenance, repairs and operation thereof.'
Manifest Objections.
1.	An undertaking entirely provincial and essentially for municipal services in its nature is removed from provincial and municipal control.
2.	Existing railways whose very existence depended on the consent of the municipality interested are without the consent of such-municipality entirely removed from municipal jurisdiction, and become1 clothed with the powers, privileges and independence of a great state line. A revolution is created in the control and conditions of the streets of municipalities.
3.	An intolerable conflict of legislative powers is precipitated-provincial rights and those of important municipal councils disregarded and local sources of revenue abolished-and it must hereafter be recognized that should this Bill become law it is open to other promoters to go from parliament to legislature, or vice versa, in an attempt to obtain greater powers, or to evade contracts and obligations entered into.
4.	The result must be that these local lines will practically be operated and maintained

just as the company desires. Imagine an ap-lication with its attendant cost being made to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council by the city of Hamilton to have a certain car declared to be out of repair and unfit to be operated on the street railway system of that city, or one by the county of York that a small section of the road bed of the Metropolitan Railway Company was out of repair-and on the other hand consider the unreasonableness of expecting that the Dominion authorities could efficiently oversee and look after the many auestions trivial in themselves, but, of large importance to the municipality, which necessarily arise in connection with ' the maintenance, repair and operation ' of a city or rural street car service.	.
5.	All the paramount powers of a state railway are vested in this extensive tramway without going into detail it is only necessary to refer to the very extensive powers of expropriation- the absolute right to build branches up to a distance of a quarter of a mile-and with the consent of the railway committee, up to six miles-the absolute right td remove trees to a distance of six rods from either side of the railway-to divert streams, change position of gas and water pipes, sewers or drains, and telegraph, telephone or electric light wires or poles, and the right to appoint constables, all of which are given to the proposed company by the Railway Act. 6, W-H-Y ?
Why should the company in the case of future friction with Toronto or Hamilton have the right to level every shade tree, whether on or off the streeet, to a distance of six rods from its railway ?
Why should the company have the right to cover the streets of either of these cities with lines under the name of branches ?
Why should the difference in principle between steam railways owning and occupying separate rights of way and railways occupying the highways belonging to the municipality, be lost sight of and obliterated ?
Why should the portions of the county of York on the highways of which railways have been already constructed under the safeguards of proper agreements, ask that all extensions of such railways, rural or urban, shall be as to ' maintenance, repair and operation,' only controlled by the provisions of the Railway Act, while they protect themselves by proposing to continue by an amendment the operation of , their agreements 7
By section 600 of the Municipal Act of Ontario, municipal councils obtain jurisdiction over the streets in the municipality, and section 601 vests every such highway in the municipality - Why should this jurisdiction be transferred to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council ?
Tha Ontario Railway Act, the Ontario Electric Railway Act, and the Ontario Street Railway Act have all declared that no railway constructed under their provisions shall be carried along a highway without the consent of the interested municipality. Why should these provisions be over-ridden, and the power therein contained transferred from municipal councils [DOT] to a railway committee or board by declaring a work similar in character to be for the general advantage of Canada 7
The right of the Dominion parliament to so Interfere cannot be supported except possibly after the declaration that this undertaking is for the advantage of Canada.
It is respectfully submitted that this declaration cannot fairly be made. At the very most all that can he pretended is that the work may
be for the benefit of portions of the counties of York. Peel. Halton and Wentworth-counties already well provided with electric railways constructed or under construction. In any event it is with much confidence submitted that the right to decide just what is best in the interest of the locality, the right of home rule, should be left with the people of the locality and the provincial parliament, who it is submitted have not proved themselves unworthy to discharge that trust.

The signatures to this document will show that the protest has the endorsation of the municipal authorities of some of the leading cities of the Dominion. It is proposed that this parliament should remove the jurisdiction over these railways from the provincial power and from the control of the municipalities interested. That was never contemplated in the Confederation Act, and yet provincial rights are constantly going by the board, and all under a Liberal administration, whose leading principle used to be the upholding of provincial rights. Just before dinner the Minister of Railways made a reference to the city of Toronto in a somewhat sneering way.
Oh, no.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
He said it was some kind of a very superior city and people up there. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that the people of Toronto are inoculated with the doctrine called public ownership, and as the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has said, they hope in a very short time to own and control the street railway of Toronto. But if legislation of this kind is allowed to go through this parliament, this franchise will not be worth a single cent. The city of Toronto derives $250,000 a year revenue from its street railway ; it hopes soon to derive $500,000, and it hopes within twenty-one years to own and control that street railway and to give the people a better and cheaper service. If you pass legislation of this kind at Ottawa, by which you are openly raiding municipal and provincial rights, you will deprive Toronto and all other cities of this fine revenue. It is a

shame to see the way a number pf the cities of this Dominion have been raided by the legislature. Down in Quebec the street railway corporations and the electric corporations of all kinds have raided the cities and have obtained powers they ought not have obtained, and it is now proposed to still further raid the cities in the federal legislature and to rob them of their inherent municipal rights.
There is something wrong surely. I have read the protest of the municipalities against their being robbed of valuable franchises in the interest of private corporations. Surely the people have a right to ask that their municipal rights be protected against these rich corporations. Let me tell the Minister of Railways that there are two kinds of confiscation, notwithstanding that the only kind he can see is the confiscation of the rights of corporations. Let me tell him that you can confiscate as well the rights of the people, and that is what you are doing here, and that is what it is the duty of the minister to prevent. He must lay down a principle that will govern not only this Toronto and Hamilton Railway, but which will govern all these other corporations who are now beginning to believe that the easiest way to accomplish their ends in raiding the municipalities is to get past the municipal council, get past the provincial legislature, and come to Ottawa, where they believe they will get everything they want. This has got to be such a menace that the municipal organizations have formed an association to defend their rights, and we find them circulating amongst members of parliament the document which I have read. It is high time that a protest was entered and that the House and the country should know that a constitutional revolution is taking place by which municipal rights and provincial, rights for that matter are being invaded by this federal parliament. It is incumbent on the minister to declare on behalf of the government that this Dominion parliament will not allow municipal rights to be invaded by corporations who come to Ottawa as a last resort, when they cannot obtain what they want from the municipalities and the provincial legislatures. I trust the minister will not make merely an amendment which will.protect one street railway, but that he will make a clear-cut announcement that this parliament of Canada cannot be used for the purpose of overriding the will of the provinces and the municipalities. If some provision of this kind is not made, the city of Toronto and other cities will be robbed of their power to grant franchises and robbed of the rights which as municipalities they should possess.
In the end we will find the province of Ontario and the other provinces turned over to these corporations with perpetual charges and franchises. That is the danger.

Under this Act, as the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has pointed out, you give these corporations perpetual franchises through the rulings of this board of railway commissioners. At present every one of them has a limited franchise, subject to termination after a number of years, and for the enjoyment of which they pay liberal allowances to the munici- , palities, and for which they are being educated to pay larger rentals. The city of Toronto to-day, if it could recover its street franchise, would give a million dollars for it; the city of Hamilton would like to get back its franchise; probably the county of York would like to get the franchise it has given to the Metropolitan Railway. But if the owners of these railways understand that the way to get past the municipalities and the provincial laws is to come to the federal parliament and have these works declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, so that the board of railway commissioners could step in and interfere with them, I say good-bye to provinciai rights and to our federal union, for the day has arrived, brought about by the action of the Liberal party, when practically the doctrine of a legislative union has been established in this country, with one supreme legislature and no other in it.

I must say I am exceedingly pleased to hear the hon. gentleman give us the assurances he has given us to-night.
I am glad to know that, after a long period of slumber, he has at last awakened to the importance and necessity of arousing parliament and the country to the imperative need of wise and safe legislation in this direction.
I hope my hon. friend is not going to relapse into that comatose condition, speaking in a political and legislative sense, in which he has existed for so long a time; for I think this parliament and the country would be relieved if we could get an assurance from him that from this time forward he is going to conduct himself with a greater measure of propriety and with some regard for the public interest; that he is going to see that the legislation passed in this House shall reflect no discredit upon it, and is going to exhaust the utmost measure of his great abilities to see that the people's rights are protected to the remotest.degree. My hon. friend must not be content with getting up for a few minutes and making these declarations and calling upon other people; but he must live up to the promises he has made, and to the expectations which no-doubt his remarks have aroused among the members of this House, and which, when known in the country, they will no doubt arouse throughout Canada. As my hon. friend has started in a judicious direction, I want to see my hon. friend, with that boundless energy which distinguishes him,

that great foresight which he possesses, that keen perception of right and wrong for which he is so well known, stand up manfully and help the government in this movement as he has not hitherto felt it his duty, and his inclination to do. I am going to ask my hon. friend, in the spirit in which he has spoken to-night, to lend me his valuable support towards correcting this amendment, so that we may have the law in perfect shape, so that we may have the people's rights in every particular protected; and while we are protecting them, and protecting corporate rights, and seeing that the municipalities are not trodden under the heel of these ruthless corporations who are seeking to swallow up other people's properties, rights and interests, I want him to assist me in an equally strong effort to secure the rights of individuals. I am going to propose an amendment which I think will meet with general acceptance ;
Nothing in this Section shall deprive the company of rights conferred upon it by any special Act of parliament of Canada heretofore passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That takes the place of the other ?
Yes, I am going to withdraw the other amendment altogether.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow me to offer a suggestion '! Why does he not make the clause say : ' Nothing in this Act shall interfere with the rights of the municipalities ' ? Do not protect the companies. Protect the municipalities; that is what we want.

Has my hon. friend reached this point, that whilst he is desirous of protecting the municipalities, those bodies which are well able to protect themselves, he will allow individuals to suffer and individual rights be trampled under foot ? When parliament has conferred a franchise or a right, will he be prepared to ask parliament to withdraw that franchise after interests have been created and grown up under it ? My hon. friend will not, I trust, forget the eloquent appeal which he made to us a few minutes ago.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I beg to call the hon. minister's attention to this fact. In his amendment he proposes to leave at large all acts which have been passed before this Act becomes law. I think during this session there have been some hundred Acts of parliament passed already. I do not think the hon. gentleman addressed his mind to this difficulty when this subject was introduced into parliament. But I would like, on the general question, to quote again from this letter with regard to the Montreal Terminal Company. The right given to it by this parliament was ' to run over such ,
streets in the city of Montreal as are designated by the council of the said city.' The hon. gentleman argues, perhaps with some technical legality, that that means that the city council had to give power to run over some streets. But what would any municipality understand from these words : ' and subject to such terms and conditions as are imposed on the company by the city council ' ? Is there one municipality in this Dominion that would not understand these words to give them absolute control over the company that was proposing to lay tracks on its streets ? We find that when this matter came before the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, that body, according to this letter, seemed to think that the city must be reasonable, that it could not impose terms that would be unreasonable. In other words, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or the board of railway commissioners acting in their place, would be the judges of whether the municipality was imposing reasonable conditions or not; and if the municipality in their opinion was acting unreasonably, the board could tell them what was reasonable. In other words, the board would be the body that would dictate on what terms the railway would be constructed through the streets of the city. I understand that one difficulty which the Railway Committee of the Privy Council found in this case was that the city wanted to impose on the Terminal Railway company conditions more onerous than had been granted to another company. Why should thSy not ? Why should not a municipality impose any conditions it thinks proper ? In one year conditions may change. A year ago a city may have made a blunder by granting a railway company power to run along its streets on too liberal terms. Is it to be bound for all time by what it does one year ? If the year after it wants to impose more onerous terms, why should it not have the right to do so, and why should the board of railway commissioners or the Railway Committee of the Privy Council undertake to discuss whether the municipality was seeking to impose unreasonable terms or not ? Beyond question the moment you put in an Act of parliament that the municipality shall have the right to dictate the terms and conditions upon which a company shall enter a city, you give that municipality the absolute power to say whether that company shall enter the city at all. Because this House chooses, without rhyme or reason, to insert into an Act that a particular work is a work for the general advantage of Canada, should it have jurisdiction in such matters. Surely it was never contemplated that the mere insertion of these words would or ought to give jurisdiction where, under the constitutional Act, none was intended to be given. It was intended only that a work should be declared for the general advan-

tage of Canada when it was really a Dominion work, and. that in that case alone the declaration should be made and this parliament should have jurisdiction. But under the loose legislation that we have been passing, these words have been inserted into statutes in order to withdraw jurisdiction from the provinces over purely local concerns and vest it in this parliament without any reasonable ground for doing so.

The more this question is discussed, the more important it appears and the more fully we realize the great variety of interests affected. It involves certainly the question of provincial rights. This is not the only Bill that raises in a very distinct form the question of provincial rights. If we go back to preceding sessions, we shall find a number of other instances which show that we are gradually raising again the old issue of provincial rights. This measure is an encroachment, not only on provincial, but municipal rights as well. With regard to the municipalities, there can be no more serious proposition perhaps than the one involved in the question raised this afternoon. True, the hon. minister proposes to modify the attitude he took earlier in the session, but even with that modification we are not dealing with the case upon a proper basis. In the cases of the cities and towns, we have perhaps grappled with the most serious phase of the question, but next in importance are,the rights of the incorporated villages and townships. Many of the electric railways may be converted into steam f-ailways, and we are confronted with this proposition, that in the future we may have the miles of electric tramways now upon our highways, highways which belong to the municipalities and were made by the municipalities and were intended primarily for the use of the people-we may have these electric lines converted into steam railways and locomotive engines puffing up and down our municipal highways.

Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say seriously that if a company is chartered to operate an electric road, it can, of its own sweet will, change its system into a steam railway line and run locomotives upon the public highway ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Those of us who have even a slight acquaintance with these matters know perfectly well that it is an easy step to change an electric railway into a steam railway. The Metropolitan Railway is to-day purchasing steam engines to run on its tracks.
They cannot do it without permission.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I admit that, but it is entering the thin end of the wedge. As my

hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) has said, we are upon the eve of a revolution in the system which has governed in this country in the past. Why, how astounded the people would be if it had been proposed in the first instance to have a steam railway run for even a few miles along the highways. And yet, we have the fact that in the old and populous county of York, the Metropolitan Company is running along what was the best highway in the Dominion of Canada, Yonge street, and they are making preparations to-day to propel their cars by steam. Now, this matter, as 1 say, is probably of primary importance to the cities. But, as regards the local municipalities it is of great importance too, and it will be a serious question throughout the length and breadth of this country for all the local municipalities, for the incorporated villages and townships as well as for the cities. What are we proposing to do ? We are proposing to vest in a board of three members the right to say, in defiance of the wishes of the municipalities, whether an electric railway or tramway shall be operated upon their highways or not. I submit that that is a proposition which, when it is realized by the people, they will never submit to. It is revolutionary. I believe it to be one of the most serious innovations that have been proposed by the government at any time ; and, so far as I am concerned, I shall oppose it in toto. The Minister of Railways says that we must not hamper the railway companies ; that we must make some provision that will safeguard the interest of the companies that have already been chartered, or we shall be encroaching on vested interests and hampering these railway companies in negotiating their securities. Which is the question of paramount importance, the facility with which these railway companies negotiate their securities, or the rights of the people who live along the lines on which it is proposed that these railways shall run ? I submit that the people who live in these rural municipalities, who live in these villages, jire the best judges of the needs of these townships and villages, and it is for their representatives, not for a board of three persons, however eminent they may be, to consider whether it is in the interest of the municipality that these railways should be run within their confines or not. It is upon the decision of the people of the locality that the matter should ultimately rest. The hon. gentleman thinks that we must consider vested rights. But there is a broad distinction to be drawn between vested rights that have been exercised and assumed, and vested rights of which the companies have first knowledge from the discussion of the matter upon the floor of this House. What we have been doing throughout the discussion of this Bill in more than one instance is suggesting, by legislative sanction, that these companies should encroach more and more upon the

rights of the people, suggesting to them to claim rights that they never dreamed of before. The hon. minister has only heard of one company, he says, that has encroached upon the rights of the municipality. I will promise the minister that if this legislation passes in the form he proposes, there will be a great crop of such encroachments upon the rights of municipalities. That will be the effect of the legislation the hon. gentleman proposes. The question of exclusive control within the cities of the valuable franchises existing there has been so ably dealt with by hon. gentlemen who lia ve given it special consideration that I do not propose to discuss it further. But 1 do suggest that in the case of municipalities outside the cities and towns they also have very valuable franchises in their roads and highways, and these should not be left to be dealt with by a board sitting in Ottawa. An important point was certainly raised by the minister when he suggested that possibly, in some instances, the representatives of the municipalities could not be induced to let the railway company use the highway upon fair terms. I am quite free to admit that there may be instances in which an extreme position is taken in that regard. But whether is it safer to leave that to the council of the municipality who can be changed, and will be changed by the people when they cease to represent fairly the views of the municipality, or, to vest it in a board composed of three men remote from'the municipality, knowing nothing of the local interests or local requirements, out of touch with the people, and having no ear for the needs of the locality. I submit that it is vastly more in the general interest of the people that, those who are in touch with local interests, the municipal council, who can be deposed if they cease to voice the views of their constituents, should be left in control of these matters rather than that such control should be handed over to a board which cannot be held to similar responsibility by those whose interests are most deeply affected.

I would like to ask the hon. minister a question with respect to the point involved. I have a letter from Joseph Burton, Esq., the reeve of Toronto township, which is a township in Peel county, lying between the city of Toronto and the city of Hamilton. The Toronto and Mimico Railway Company applied to the legislature of the province of Ontario at its last session, and secured a charter to run a road between Toronto and Hamilton through this township. My correspondent tells me that in that charter the rights were left with the municipalities to say where the road should be built through the township. What I want to ask the hon. minister is, will the amendment he proposes take away that right from the municipality of that township ?	,

It would not affect it-would not have any relation to it at all. This does not relate to any company incorporated by a provincial legislature, except so far as crossings with Dominion lines are concerned. It will not affect the question in the slightest degree.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand, then, that the rights that were allowed to remain in the municipality referred to, by the charter granted by the local legislature of Ontario at its last session, will not be interfered with by the amendment that the minister is now proposing.
It will not affect them at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Supposing that a railway company comes down here and gets itself declared to be a railway for the general advantage of Canada, won't these rights be interfered with unless he puts in the word ' municipalities ' ?
W'hen they come down here we will be in a better position to judge.
speakername: Tins MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister should be informed of the facts. There is a Bill now passing through the House having for its object the amalgamation or grouping together a lot of these tram lines, one of which is to run between Toronto and Hamilton to connect with the Hamilton Radial system. Now my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) asks this question : That being one of the group of trains that are to be absorbed by this company which now has a Bill before parliament, if its enterprise should be declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, will not the rights of the municipality to which he has referred be taken from it ? In case that Bill passes through this House and the company is declared to be incorporated for the purpose of constructing a road that is for the general advantage of Canada, will not the rights of the municipality be interfered with ?
I do not know what Bill the hon. gentleman refers to, but has there been auy Bill before this parliament which proposes to absorb a number of lines ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, and it will come up to-morrow night as a private Bill.
The hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) introduced it.

Has the legislature given the other companies the power to sell to this company ? Unless we assume by a distinct declaration that it has a control over these local lines, they would not have any power to sell unless their charter gave it to them, or some amending Act of the provincial legislature.

Mr, LANCASTER. This Bill coming up to-morrow niglit asks for power to purchase a certain number of railways, one of which is the Hamilton, Beamsville and Grimsby road incorporated by the Ontario legislature. It got permission to run on their highway by certain regulations and under certain conditions only, and if it does not conform to those conditions it can be put off that highway. Now, if this Bill coming up to-morrow night passes, and that railway is given permission to sell out to this Toronto and Hamilton Railway, I ask the minister if it is not the case, unless this section is made to cover other municipalities as well as cites and towns, that the rights which the townships of Barton, Saltfleet, Grimsby, Clinton and others nows possess, townships through which this railway runs, will go by the board ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There seems to be so much doubt about the interpretation and meaning of the clause that we are discussing, that I would like to be clear about it. In the city of Montreal we have two street railway companies to which we have granted certain privileges and rights. They have undertaken to do certain things, one of which, for instance, is to remove in the winter all the snow from the streets. 1 would like to know if the Bill passes in its present shape, whether any conditions that may have been imposed by the city of Montreal, or that we may deem proper to impose later on, will be affected ?

They would not be interfered with by this Bill.
Hon, Mr. TARTE. Then we would have tlie right to impose any other conditions that we saw fit ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
You will have all the rights you have heretofore had, whatever they are.
Hon. Mr. TARTE, It will not interfere with the conditions we have imposed ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
In the city of Toronto there is a limited street railway franchise. Approaching the city of Toronto are four or five suburban lines, and there is now a proposal to consolidate them and have them declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. Under that consolidation they propose to ask this parliament, or this board of railway commissioners, the right to run to the centre of the city of Toronto. The road that comes from the west is to come to the centre of the city, say to the city hall, and the suburban line that is coming from the east is to have the right fo come to the city hall, also the road from the north, also the road from the north-east, also the road from the north-west. These suburban roads have none of them limited franchises, they have perpetual franchises. They come Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
to the centre of Toronto, they are declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, they are united into one line and thenceforward they are entrenched and in possession of the streets of Toronto for ever without the leave or consent of the city, and the franchise which the city owns in its street railways is done for for ever, and the city will never get a dollar of revenue thereafter.
