All these things are in the minds of these railway companies to-day, they have them all in view, they are trying to secure these things from the provincial legislature, they are trying to get them by surreptitious means from this parliament, by asking to be declared a road for the general advantage of Canada. Why, look at what took place in the city of TOronto the other night. The very same people who are now attempting to consolidate these suburban roads, raided the city fhe other night and tried to take possession of our streets in the middle of the night, had fifty men at work, and if the mayor and the authorities had not been alert they would have been in possession to-day, and would have thereby prepared the way for this very broad proposition that they have in hand. So there is a danger of the municipal rights of cities in these franchises being taken away from the people by this Bill. The constitution of Canada never contemplated that. There was no legislation of this kind introduced in the old days into this parliament. But now the provincial authorities in Canada have said that their rights are being raided. They themselves are to blame. There is a way of stopping many of these companies from coming from under provincial jurisdiction to Dominion jurisdiction, and that is by putting in provincial legislation some kind of a clause providing that if they go to the higher legislature, their rights already obtained shall become null and void. Some legislatures are protecting themselves in that way. I am not giving an imaginary case; I am giving! the actual facts showing what Is taking place in the city of Toronto to-day and that Is the reason why the municipal authorities are aroused, why they have organized, why they are before this parliament hnd why they intend to ask that this Bill which is coming up to-morrow be defeated. I trust the hon. minister will hold this clause over and that he will give the municipalises an opportunity of being heard, and especially, not only in connection with this clause, but in connection with this Bill, that he will be prepared to assure the municipalities of all portions of this Dominion that therd is no intention on the part of the government or of parliament either through this Railway Bill or any special Bill to in any way deprive them of the control which they ought to have over their own streets and over their own franchises within their respective limits. What I say as to cities is equally true also to other municipalities, whether it be a township, village or any other corporation.

As tlie matter lias been discussed very largely in reference to the Toronto and Hamilton Railway Bill, I may be permitted to say a word or two on the subject. I do not think this is the proper time to discuss the Bill and I do not intend to discuss it, but the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) and other hon. gentlemen who have spoken have discussed that Bill and have placed it unfairly before the committee. One would imagine that all the discussion was on the rights of the city of Toronto and that it was the only municipality in the world to be considered. I want to say that every one of the municipalities surrounding Toronto is anxious for the passage of the Toronto and Hamilton Railway Bill. Every single one is anxious for the passage of that Bill, not in its present shape, but as it is proposed to amend it.
By whom ?

By the promoter of the Bill. When the proper time comes, as hon. gentlemen know very well, that Bill is to be amended. The amendment has been submitted to every municipality surrounding Toronto, and every municipality approves of it and is anxious for the passage of the Bill. It seems to me, that, if the hon. gentleman had been as anxious as he pretends to be now for the rights of the municipalities, he would have been in his place when this Bill was considered. It was introduced on the 5th of May, read a second time on the 12th of May, referred to the Railway Committee, stood on the Order paper for a month, notice was given of the meeting of the special day fixed for the consideration of the Bill in the Railway Committee, and when the Bill came up, where was the hon. member for East York? Away at work on his farm neglecting the duties which he is paid to attend to here. Where wTere the four members from the city of Toronto ? There was not a solitary one of them in attendance at the committee ; not one of them paid any attention to tbe committee.
Where was the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell)- raiding the city of Toronto ?

The hon. member for West York wns in his place in the committee defending the rights of the municipalities as he has always been found in his right place. I was not away neglecting my duties and drawing my pay for doing it as the hon. member for East York was. The question has resolved itself into this : There are two parties to this Bill. There are first the municipalities around the city of Toronto.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I wish to ask your ruling whether it is proper to anticipate
an order on the paper by discussing it before we reach it ?

Before you rule, Mr. Chairman, I just want to say that I am discussing the particular Bill that has been referred to so often by the hon. member for East York and the hon. member for 'Hamilton (Mr. Barker) who have been discussing it. I am discussing the principle, and I want to show why the amendment which is proposed by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals is in the interest of the municipalities of this country and why it is an amendment that should be adopted by parliament. I am illustrating that by the reference that has been made by the hon. gentlemen who preceded me to the Bill of the Toronto and Hamilton Railway Company. The Bill to which reference has been made involves two points.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As my ruling has been asked, I may say that references were made to this Bill, and I regarded them as illustrations of the point which hon. gentlemen were discussing in regard to municipal control. If the references were so intended they were perfectly within the rules of the House. But, to discuss the merits of a Bill which will come before us to-morrow is beyond the rules of the House and the Bill in that sense cannot be discussed.

I quite agree with your ruling, Mr. Chairman. I was not proposing to discuss the Bill except in its application to the matter now before the committee. The point has been raised in behalf of the municipality of Toronto, for instance, that no railway should go into the city unless by the sanction and approval of tin* municipality. I take the ground that whatever rights you give to the city of Toronto you must give to every other municipality in the country. The municipalities have just as good a right to have whatever protection is required. The municipality of Scarborough, of Etobicoke, Toronto township or any other municipality should have the same rights as are given to the great city of Toronto. Where are you going to be landed ? Suppose a great railway work is projected that is in the general interests of the country and you place it in the hands of any little tu'penny ha'penny municipality on the whole line to hold it up and stop the whole work ? I say it is not right. These railways, and this is the amendment which will be proposed to the Bill to which reference has been made, should first be required to obtain the consent of the municipality having jurisdiction over the highways. But if a municipality refuses to give that consent, or if they cannot get its sanction, then, they should have the right to appeal to the railway commissioners who are disinterested men, whose duty it is to take charge of these matters. Or, you may

refer it to the bight court if you like. The rule has been heretofore to refer the question to the Governor in Council and the Governor in Council has always sanctioned any proper request and done what was right and proper in the interests of the people. I expect that the commissioners who will be appointed under this Railway Bill will be men above reproach and men who thoroughly understand all these questions. If they do not know it will be their duty to go and find out. They will consult the city of Toronto, they will consult the municipalities interested and they will take into consideration all the rights and privileges and look thoroughly into the case and I am sure that they will give a decision that will be in the interest of the people at large. But I want to point out that if the proposition of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is carried into effect it will place it in the power of any one municipality to block any great railway enterprise that is in the interest of the whole country. The promoters of such an enterprise may get the consent of fifty municipalities and the fifty-first will say : You cannot get through this municipality, and the railway is blocked. I do not think that is in the interest of the country, much as I believe in protecting and guarding the rights of municipalities, and I know that under the railway commissioners all the rights and privileges that should be accorded to the municipalities will be ensured to them, the terms upon which the company shall operate upon the streets, the amount of money they shall pay, the amount of roadway they shall keep up, the percentage that shall accrue to the municipality, all these things will be taken into consideration and justice will be done to all. I think the amendment pro-proposed by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals is one that is in the interest of the country and ought to receive the sanction of this committee.

The clause proposed by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals Iras two very serious objections. The first is, that it proposes to protect the rights of cities and towns, but not of incorporated villages or rural municipalities. I agree with the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) that there is just as strong reason for protecting the rights of incorporated villages and rural municipalities as there is for protecting the rights of cities and towns. In this respect that clause falls short. My second objection is that it proposes to protect the rights of railway companies under existing charters, quite regardless of whether these rights were properly or improperly obtained. I have been amused often at the contention of those who cry out vested rights when they come here. I have been amused I say at their contention because in my opinion it is not confiscation to denude them of so called vested rights which Mr. CAMPBELL.
I
have been improperly acquired. In the first place they got these vested rights through our invading the rights of the municipalities or of the provinces as the case may be. It is we who did the confiscation for them originally. As a member of this parliament for many years I have watched with a great deal of interest the trend of legislation here. Twenty years ago we had jealous defenders of provincial rights, but to-day they are silent. It was with pride and pleasure that twenty years ago I saw almost every member of the province of Quebec jealously guarding provincial rights, but those who have taken their places to-day seem to hold provincial rights as of little value. None were more strenuous defenders of provincial rights than the Ontario reformers of twenty years ago, but Where are they to-day ? I have heard it said over and over again in this House, when It was proposed to declare that a work was for the general advantage of Canada, that we could not take away provincial rights by that mere declaration. Many eminent lawyers have held that view. But to-day, fortified by the decisions of our courts, we believe that whenever we say a work is for the general advantage of Canada, that declaration is sufficient to deprive the provinces of their constitutional rights in that corporation. We have been practically confiscating rights belonging to the provinces ; we have been surrounding the provinces with chains, and to-day we are endeavouring to weld the links so as to bind them for ever. That is just what the proposition of the Minister of Railways and Canals will do. He declares that when a railway has acquired rights, whether they be properly or improperly obtained, we will not interfere with them. . Well, whether you call it eonficsation or socialism or whatever you care to call it,
I publicly declare here that I have no respect for rights which are improperly obtained, and as a member of parliament and a member of this commonwealth, I would take away these rights and restore them to those to whom they properly belong. I have always regarded that as wrong, and what was wrong twenty years ago cannot be right to-day.
You thought it was right then.

I did not. I have voted against it persistently and consistently for twenty-five years, and I regret to see that many Liberals who fought side by side with me on this issue twenty years ago are now amongst the most willing to invade the rights of the provinces.
You did not always vote that way.

If the hon. member was better informed he would know that there is no truth iu the senseless interruption he makes. I never interrupt the hon. gentle-

man, and I dislike these interruptions that are not founded upon common sense. If the hon. gentleman knew my record in this House he would not make the statement he has made, but on the contrary he would give me credit for consistency in this, as he might fairly do in other things. Let me give an example of interference with municipal rights. They are building a line of railway in Winnipeg which runs twenty miles out in the country, and wherever there is a depression in the street I found the street railway was building an embankment to keep their track on a level that must greatly interfere with the drainage of the surface water from the street. I do not know whether they are working under a provincial or Dominion charter, but if it be a provincial charter the people of the municipalities are remiss in their duty. When I asked why they allowed such a thing to be done the answer was : They are working under a charter and we cannot interfere with them. This railway runs through rural municipalities, and it is a living example of how rural municipalities may be seriously injured by the operations of these corporations. I hold, Sir, that we should protect the rights of these rural municipalities just as well as the rights of the cities. I object to this proposal of the Minister of Railways and Canals because It perpetuates rights that were improperly obtained. I object to it because it does not protect the rights of the rural municipalities; and I object to it because it is an infringement of the rights which the provinces should enjoy under the constitution.

I had not the opportunity of hearing this motion read, but I would like to know if it is a fact that a railway can go along a highway in any municipality without the permission of that municipality? If that be the case I hope the minister will amend it. In the county of Jacques Cartier where I live, we have a road there only wide enough for two carriages to pass, and if a railway should be permitted to go along that narrow road it would block the entire traffic. I do not think that is what the minister intends.
It is.
If it be, then I hope that the minister will amend the clause so that they will at least have to get the consent of my municipality before doing such a thing.
And every other municipality.
Well, I am speaking for my own parish in particular.

I do not mean anything of the kind, and I hope that I have made it clear on more than one occasion that I do not mean anything of the kind. What we are
doing here is passing a law which shall have reference solely and exclusively to federal charters and to the railway companies incorporated under federal charters. We are not proposing by this legislation to interfere in the slightest degree with the legislation of any of the provinces. I want hon. members to keep that in their minds. The question as to whether or not this parliament has wisely exercised its powers in declaring local works to be for the general advantage of Canada, and thereby acquiring control over provincial charters, is a question altogether outside of this Bill. We are not proposing to do it here. I quite agree with what many hon. gentlemen have said, that that power has been exercised too freely in the past. But whose fault is that ? is it the fault of any one party in this House in times past ? I think not.
Mr, MACLEAN. Yes. The government have
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
My hon. friend will pardon me. I say no, and my hon. friend will find it difficult to establish it. I believe there has been no division of party lines upon that question-never ; and why ? Because the question has not been raised ; because parties have applied here for legislation, and members of committees and the Committee of the Whole, when it came before them, have allowed the legislation to pass. Those who have been opposed to that legislation may reflect upon themselves, but they have no right to reflect upon any one else. They have no right to claim exemption for themselves or for any one political party, nor to claim the right to criticise the action of their opponents. The question has not hitherto attracted the same amount of attention that it attracts now, because the people who desired incorporation for what were merely provincial purposes have been coming to parliament very frequently of late. There has been a disposition to come to parliament for these powers, for some reason or other, and these applications have multiplied so rapidly that they have aroused, no doubt legitimately, a strong feeling against the practice. I am prepared to assist any member of this committee, when a Bill of that kind comes up, to strike out the clause declaring the work to be . for the general advantage of Canada, unless good reasons are given why it should be so declared ; and the members who sit on the right hand of the Speaker will not yield to those who sit on the other side in their declarations in that regard. I see a very weak and flimsy, and I do not think very creditable, attempt by some hon. members on the other side of the House to make political capital by representing themselves to be the only people who care anything about municipal interests, and by spending hour after hour in speechifying on the subject when no body was controverting the position they

took, in order that their remarks might be spread out on 'Hansard.' I exonerate some of the hon. gentlemen opposite from this charge; but the gentlemen who have been doing this are not of the same size as others. I say they want to spread their speeches out on 'Hansard,' in order that they may send them out among their constituents to show how they have been standing up for the rights and liberties of the people as against those fellows on the other side of the House, although it would puzzle any man among them to find anybody opposing them. I do not claim that we on this side of the House art any more zealous in that particular. I admit that lion, gentlemen opposite desire that proper legislation should be placed on the statute-book in reference to these matters. I am willing to acknowledge that, and they will, if they desire to be fair, acknowledge that we on this side are just as anxious in the same direction. This is a very weak attempt, I say, on the part of some lion, gentlemen opposite to parade themselves before the country as the bold and valiant defenders of the peoples' rights as against their opponents-a vain attempt. I do not believe that, when they come to count up the result, they will count many noses. The people know how cheap such an attempt is. We have a Bill here which we are trying to make as good a Bill as we can make it; and I think my hon. friends opposite, barring this little disposition which exists on the part of some, have the same desire. I know that some lion, gentlemen opposite would like to create the impression that this Bill would have come out of this committee in a most deplorable shape if it had not been for the important assistance they rendered in its preparation. I know that some of my hon. friends are not making these long speeches for nothing. After it is all over, I know that they will make large claims in respect of what they have done. My hon. friends on this side of the House, you will observe, are not making long speeches-why ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Because the minister is doing it.

I will tell you why. They are not so anxious to hear themselves talk ; and in the next place, they have done in hosts what has only been done by individuals on the other side. They have taken means of calling my attention, during the long period that this Bill has been under consideration, to jioints which they would like to have covered, and to improvements which they would like to have made, and the record of their work appears in the many amendments which have been made to the Act. I have availed myself of the suggestions of members who came to me privately, whose sole desire was not limited to the opportunity of making a speech. They wanted to see Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
the legislation improved, my hon. friends on the other side of the House have been equally zealous, I will not say more zealous ; and the fruit of their effort has appeared without their making any great show in ' Hansard ' or on the floor of parliament. We are going to have this Bill in pretty good shape; but it could not emerge from this committee in good shape if we were all of the disposition of my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule). My hon. friend has had a long experience in parliament, and lie knows that the credit of this parliament cannot be sustained if, after we confer a right on any individual in this country, on the strength of which he has invested his means or his friends have invested their means, we propose to take that right away, be the consequences what they may.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We are doing it in every session of parliament.

We are not doing it this session. My hon. friend thinks we might do it properly. My hon. friend would do it without hesitation. I would not do it. The vast majority of this House would hesitate to do it, and I am quite sure that no interest that could possibly be involved would justify us in doing it. The question about which all this talk has taken place is not whether we are going to tread with the iron heel on some municipal authority, or sweep away the rights of any municipal body, or interfere with the freedom of any body ; but the question is, shall we, in enlarging and extending the power of the municipality, make it subject to this one limitation, that if any rights have been conferred upon Individuals by this parliament, those rights shall not, in the working out if this Bill, and in the interpretation and construction of this law, be taken away from them. If any rights have been conferred toy this parliament, those rights shall not, in the working out of this Bill, aud the interpretation of this clause, be taken away from them. I do not think that the subject is one which would justify a very great deal more discussion than we have had. Our minds must be pretty well made up, and I hardly think that anything more need be said.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Hon. members on this side must l'eel under a great debt of gratitude to the hon. gentleman for the fatherly advice he has given us in such a kindly spirit. I assure him that we appreciate it cordially and heartily. Would he now permit a very humble member from this side to make a suggestion to him ?
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
We appreciate the great amount of labour he has given to make this Bill as perfect as possible. When we saw

occasion for it, we offered suggestions. We have not gone behind the door to do so, but at the right time and place, when the House was in committee and the hon. gentleman and his supporters had the right to criticise our suggestions, we have expressed our opinions and offered amendments when we found what we believed to have been flaws in the Bill. We did so in the most respectful and friendly way. Some of our amendments were accepted in the best possible spirit by the hon. minister, and we believe that he accepted them because he considered they would improve his measure. We feel confident that the hon. minister is actuated solely by the desire to make this Bill as perfect as possible. In his closing remarks, the hon. gentleman said that what he proposed to do was to secure to corporations the rights which they had received in years gone by from this parliament. 1 do not think that, if the hon. minister had confined himself to the amendment which he now accepts, five minutes of the time of this committee would have been occupied with any further discussion upon clause 184. What we have objected to is the fact that the hon. minister, when he entered the chamber, distributed among us a number of amendments, amongst them an amendment io clause 184, the effect of which would liave been to destroy that recognition of municipal rights which he was good enough to make some eight or ten days ago; and 1 take it that he has been so impressed with the arguments or suggestions from this side that he has gracefully withdrawn the amendment he presented in the first place and lias submitted a further amendment protecting the rights of the companies incorporated by this parliament some time ago. We on this side have no desire to take away from any company the rights it has legally acquired from any legislative body with power to grant them; and when he declared that the rights of one company, the Montreal Terminal, might be injuriously affected by the amendment he accepted ten days ago, my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) suggested that he should make a special provision to protect the rights of that company. We have not the slightest desire to interfere with whatever rights the Terminal has legally obtained, and join with the hon. gentleman in protecting them, but we thought-and the hon. gentleman will not contradict the statement-that if the amendment he presented to section 184 had been allowed to go, every municipality in tiie country would have been at the mercy of the railway commission and every municipal right might have been taken away by the action of the commissioners. The hon. minister before recess made reference to tiie city of Toronto. I do not know whether he intended to be sarcastic or flattering, but I would make this suggestion. I would, on behalf of the mayor and cor-192

poration and citizens of Toronto, invite him to come to that city and take a trip over its train-car system. All the provisions in connection with that system were prepared by the engineer and solicitor of the city, the contract was drawn by the city attorney, the system was laid down on the conditions imposed by the city, and we have the best street railway system in America today ; and I think that the municipality gets a greater revenue from it, considering its mileage and traffic, than any other municipality does from any other street railway. I do not intend to make a long speech and lie put in the category of other hon. gentlemen whom the hon. minister has chastised and stigmatised most unfairly. If the amendment which he suggested to section J84 became law, the privileges we are enjoying in Toronto to-day would practically disappear.
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me to tell him that I know something about the situation in Toronto, and I have the temerity to say that I know as much at least about it as the hon. gentleman. Let me tell him that if power were given the bbard of commissioners to allow other tramways to come into the city of Toronto, the value of the franchise we have there now would be destroyed. Because that franchise was made valuable by the fact that the company leasing it has the exclusive right to operate an electric car service into and through the city.
Does the hon. gentleman know how many companies are authorized by this parliament to lay down street railway lines in Toronto ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not know of any company.
In that case this section would not have any application to Toronto whatever.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do know that attempts are being made, and have been successfully made, to get legislation through this parliament declaring works to be for the general advantage of Canada, which are purely and entirely provincial in their nature. 1 want to tell the hon. gentleman that the sole object of these promoters in coming to this parliament and having these enterprises declared to be for the general advantage of Canada is to escape the obligations which the province and the municipalities would impose upon them. No one knows that better than the hon. minister himself. If the right to operate street railways is to be declared for the general advantage of Canada, where will legislation of this kind stop ?

It is a prostitution of the powers and prerogatives of the parliament of Canada to pass such legislation. Would the lion, gentleman seriously argue that a group of railways around the city of Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, or Condon would be a work for the general advantage of Canada and should be incorporated by this parliament ?
Will the kon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ?
When I get through, my hon. friend can follow. And I would prefer that 'he would allow me to continue my line of argument.
I do not blame him, for not wanting to get an answer.
If the hon. gentleman insists, I shall give way to him.

I would ask my hon. friend, in the most respectful manner, whether iie does not think that the proper time to guard against those things is when the particular charter is before parliament ? And is it not right that we should have a General Railway Act to deal with the different railways that are chartered by this parliament ?

The hon. gentleman twelve months ago asked me the same question, when I was making an emphatic protest against the incorporation of the Toronto Niagara Power Company. I tried to point out to him that all railways declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada will come under the purview of this commission. The hon. gentleman will admit that, in this I am right. The tram-car lines come here seeking incorporation and are declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, and the control and operation of those lines will come under the jurisdiction of the board of commission.
That is not the question I a Eked.

We are trying to protect the rights of the municipalities by the amendment to clause 184. How did that clause read before the hon. minister proposed his further amendment this afternoon ? It read as follows :
The railway may be carried upon, along or across any existing highway upon leave therefor having been first obtained from the board as hereinafter provided. But the board shall not grant leave to any company to carry any street railway or tramway or any railway operated or to be operated as a street railway or tramway along any highway which Is within the limits of any city or incorporated town until the company shall have first obtained the consent therefor by a by-law of the municipal authority of such city or incorporated town.
Though I am not a lawyer, I take it that if that clause were permitted to remain in that shape, these tram-car outfits which are declared to be works for the general Mr. CLARKE.
advantage of Canada, could not go along the streets of a municipality at all without first obtaining the consent of the municipality. That is our contention. Have we not the right to demand that protection for these particular municipalities and for all municipalities ? Is it not a reasonable proposition that where a great number of human beings are assembled in one city, one hundred and fifty, two hundred or two hundred and fifty thousand people, that their rights in the highways shall be protected ? Is this parliament more jealous of the rights of railway promoters and tramroad promoters and exploiters than it is of the rights of the people ?
Has anybody disputed that?	'
My hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Wade) I understood, disputed that.
Not at all.
Then, what was lie disputing ?

The Toronto and Niagara Power Company was not a railway company at all, but was absolutely a power company ; and the rights of municipalities were guarded in the Private Bills Committee before the Bill came back to this House.

My hon. friend has contradicted the statement I have made. Let me draw attention to the discussion that took place on the Toronto and Niagara Power Company. I drew attention, when the Bill was in the committee stage, to the fact that the gentlemen who were asking for incorpora tiou as the Toronto and Niagara Power Company were, probably by coincidence, probably by circumstances, the owners of the Toronto Railway Company, and also of the Suburban Railway companies that it is now proposed to amalgamate with the Toronto and Hamilton Company. And I drew attention to the fact that it was only reasonable that the municipalities through which the power company passed should have the right to obtain power, and that the power company should sell it to them without discrimination ; because I pointed out that the franchises, of the tramroads would fall in, and unless the company was obliged to sell power without discrimination the value of the franchises would he destroyed. And when we asked that this should be done, hon. gentlemen opposite voted against that simple proposition. Twelve months have elapsed since that charter was given. And now we find that tile gentlemen who got that charter and their associates are asking now for a charter for a railway, to be declared a work for the general advantage of Canada, to amalgamate not only the suburban railways, but the Toronto and Hamilton Railway in one company, and to over-

ride by legislation from this parliament the obligations, the duties, the conditions which the legislature of the province of Ontario imposed upon them and which the municipalities have imposed upon them. This is our position. It is a sound position, and we are not going to recede from it Hon. gentlemen opposite may think that we are wrong. They have a right to their opinion. But it is surely our bounden duty, at every stage when an opportunity offers, to protest against the Invasion of municipal rights, when we believe that that invasion is not in the public interest. The hon. minister very courteously amended this clause, No. 184, when it was before us ten or twelve days ago. The amendment the hon. gentleman agreed to did not go so far as that I suggested to him. I desired that the municipalities-all the municipalities rural or urban-should have their rights protected. The hon. gentleman confined it to the exclusion of tramroads from incorporated towns and cities. So far so good. But I say that the rights of all should be protected, that rural municipalities had rights that ought not to be disregarded, and that the object of this parliament should be to protect those rights as against the claims of railway and tram-road promoters. One word more before I resume my seat with regard to the position the city of Toronto occupies. I have already said that the franchise of the street railway belongs to the city of Toronto, but it has been leased for a period of years. The citizens of Toronto have not objected to the entrance of suburban trams. In fact, we have been tryin'g to get them in. We are building a market at an expense of more than a quarter of a million dollars to store country produce, to facilitate the business they are expected to do. But, while we want the suburban tram-car lines to come in, we want them to enter upon the lines of railway already existing, and we want them to come in upon conditions imposed by the city of Toronto. The difference that has existed between the promoters of the Toronto and Hamilton railroad and the corporation of Toronto has been that, while the citizens of Toronto desire that whatever agreement they make for the entry of the suburban roads should terminate with the lease of the Toronto franchise, the proprietors of these suburban roads had the audacity to ask that they should have the right in perpetuity to run their lines into the city of Toronto. Was that a fair proposition ? And, not being able to obtain from the provincial legislature, or from the municipality of the city of Toronto, these privileges, these unfair and unjust privileges, they come here and ask this parliament to incorporate them as a work for the general advantage of Canada and seek to override _ not only the municipal, but provincial rights. That is a statement of facts, and I challenge contradiction of it ; and 1924
I say we are only doing our duty as members of this opposition in raising our voices, however feebly and ineffectively, in favour of maintaining municipal and provincial rights and against this parliament being made the means of incorporating a purely local concern and declaring it to be for the general advantage of Canada. Mv hon. friend from West York (Mr. Campbell) said that the municipalities about Toronto were in favour of the entrance of the Toronto and Hamilton Railway.
That is not law yet.

I only refer to it as the hon. gentleman referred to it. I only want to say that the city of Toronto lias not interfered, that it has left the suburban municipalities free to make any arrangements they thought good, and I think the least the city of Toronto has a right to expect is that the suburban municipalities will allow the city to make its own agreement. The principal value of this franchise is in the right of access to the city of Toronto ; and if that is a valuable franchise the city of Toronto is the best judge as to what value to place upon it and "what terms to exact from those to whom it is conceded.
I do not propose to follow the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) in the long diatribe-
Diatribe ?

Yes, diatribe. I have chosen the word advisedly. I do not propose to follow the hon. gentleman in the long diatribe which he has chosen to inflict upon us here to-night concerning the street railways of Toronto. He has done so notwithstanding that he knows that that matter will come up to-morrow evening. But I may go one step further and tell the hon. gentleman that he never discovered the Bill known as the Toronto and Hamilton Railway was something that was going to interfere with the rights of Toronto until it had its second reading, and after it had passed the Railway Committee. The hon. member for Toronto was silent as a'091111 in its shell while that was going on until the press drew the matter to his attention. When the question of the tramways and electric railways of Toronto come before us. we shall be pleased to listen to what the hon. gentleman has to say upon the subject. But now we are discussing a general railway commission Bill, yet he wishes to discuss this question of provincial electric railways, something entirely beyond the jurisdiction of this parliament, something which I hope, and which hon. members on this side of the House hope will not be dealt with here, but will be left to the jurisdiction of the province.
Why, the Bill before us deals with them in half a dozen sections.

I admit tljat the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) lias taken a great deal of pains and a great deal of care in connection with tliis matter, out I must tell bim in tliis, as in most other sections of the Bill, be is entirely wrong. The Bill does not propose to deal with provincial electric railways-
All I want to say to the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) is that he had better read the Bill.

And all I want to say to the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) is that if he were to read the Bill half a dozen times more his ideas would be quite as beclouded as they are after the reading he has given it. The hon. member for West Toronto tells us that the Bill to incorporate the Toronto and Niagara Company usurped the rights of the streets of the city of Toronto to the absolute disregard of the rights of the citizens or the corporation of that city. I desire to draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to section 13 of the Bill of last year, which was passed before the Private Bills Committee and afterwards was passed in this House without amendment, though the hon. gentleman made a speech in connection with it. This, be it remembered, was not a tramway company, but it was for the purpose of transmitting power from Niagara Palls to the city of Toronto to supply the city, and the effect of the Bill was to give the right to erect poles and to do other works to carry out the purposes of the company. There was this express clause put in :
Provided the same are so constructed as not to incommode the public use of streets, highways or public places or to impede the ^ access to any house or other building erected in the vicinity thereof, or to interrupt the navigation of any waters, but the company shall be responsible for all damages which it causes in carrying out or maintaining any of its said works.
So that in the Bill which the hon. gentleman held up as an example, the very safeguards were put in which now at last he wakes up to say ought to be inserted in all Bills in which the public interest is concerned.

I do not propose to travel out of the record as the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Cowan) has done, but to deal directly with the question before the committee. Niow I would assure the minister that I do not intend to make a speech to circulate in my constituency, notwithstanding the statement made by the member for Essex. The amendment that was adopted by this committee to section 184, reads as follows :
But the board shall not grant leave to any company to carry any street railway or tramway, or any railway operated or to he operated as a street railway or tramway, along any high-

way which is within the limits of any city or incorporated town.
Since the minister 'has given us an assurance. that he is enlarging the powers of municipalities, I wish to ask him why he does not give the same power to townships and villages that he gives to cities and incorporated towns. Now that is what my constituents desire should be done. I have a special request that the minister be asked to extend that privilege, or right, or power, to other municipalities as well as incorporated cities and towns. If he will accede to my request, I shall make no further protest with regard to this section. I realize that he will only be granting what is our right, and I contend that the minor municipalities, the incorporated villages and townships have the same right to protection for their streets and highways as the towns and cities. Now I hope and trust that the minister, since he is endeavouring to meet the views of the committee, will enlarge the amendment by adding the words 'other municipalities.'

I asked the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) whether he did not think that the proper time to raise these objections in regard to street railways was when the charters for them were before the House. Was not that the time to ask that such conditions and provisions should he thrown around the charters as were necessary in order to protect the interests of the cities and towns ? Certainly all hon. gentlemen must recognize that we are to-night attempting to frame a general railway law, one that will apply to all railways that are in existence to-day, and to all railways that may come into existence in the future, and to street railways that may be chartered by this parliament. Now I was astonished at some of the speeches made by hon. gentlemen opposite. A stranger listening to them would suppose we were passing this clause for the first time, and he would be surprised to know that ever since Canada had a Railway Act, and long before the Dominion existed, a similar Railway Act existed in the old province of Ontario and the other provinces, in which substantially the same clause was contained as we are now discussing. Section 183 of the General Railway Act as amended in 1888, contained substantially the same provision, by which a railway company can cross a highway or, by leave of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, can go along that highway. Now, Sir, I do not take a second place to the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) or to any other hon. gentleman on that side of the House, or upon this, in my desire to protect the rights of the provinces and of the municipalities. Nobody has ever raised any such question before. These hon. gentlemen are setting up a man of straw for the purpose of knocking it down. X want to ask the hon. member for East Grey if, during all those twenty-five years he has

been sitting in this House, lie ever raised bis voice to say one word against this section 183 as it is contained in the Kailway Act ?

I can tell the hon. gentleman that twenty-one or twenty-two years ago I fought that question as vigorously as I could, when it was proposed by the same means to take over the Toronto, Grey and Bruce Kailway. I drew attention to the fact that it was a provincial railway that had been subsidized to the tune of $300,000. In one of the by-laws were contained certain provisions that were regarded as valuable for municipalities, and if that railway was amalgamated with a Dominion railway and declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, it took away provincial rights, and I fought it as vigorously as I could, as I have done many times since.

Now I wonder if the hou. gentleman has satisfied himself that he has answered my question. What I asked him wasi this, if he could tell me that he ever stood in his place in parliament and uttered one word against this section 1.83 which has been in the Railway Act ever since Canada had a Railway Act, as Infringing upon the rights of provinces or municipalities. That is what I want to get from him.

I do not remember whether I was present at the time that Act was passed. But I say that from time to time when private Bills were brought before par-liameut infringing upon those rights, I objected as strenuously as I knew how.

There is an Act upon our statute-book which is substantially the same as the section we are now trying to enact. There is this difference, that under the old section as it stood it was necessary, before you could run along a highway, to have the consent of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. Instead of that tribunal we nowhave the board and it is upon that that hon. gentlemen are making all this talk about guarding the rights of municipalities.
There was no Railway Committee of the Privy Council for years after the question was debated in this House.

The hon. gentleman is certainly taking a marvellous position. We have had the old Act amended time and time again. Let me pin him down to this that in 1888 the whole railway legislation was consolidated. Did he, when the Act was going through in 1888 and when he was upon this side of the House, rise up and say anything about infringing upon provincial rights, or city rights, or municipal rights ? Did he not sit in his place and give a silent vote, or if he spoke, did he not speak in favour of it ?
Never.

We, upon this side of the House, are getting somewhat tired of this kind of talk. It is a fact, and hon, gentlemen know it, that before a railway can be located over the country the company must come forward with their plans showing the location and get these plans approved and if these plans show a line running along the street, before they can be put into execution, they must have the approval of the board. There is a tribunal provided for by this Bill which will listen to all parties and decide as to whether it is proper to allow a railway to pass along a street in any municipality. I can imagine that in 99 cases out of 100 cases the railway company will not be allowed to build their line along the highway, but in the 99th case, or perhaps in the 999th case, it will be absolutely necessary that the railway should be carried along the highway or a street because there would be no other feasible way by which it could be carried along. Then, I ask hon. gentlemen as a reasonable proposition : Must not this parliament have the power to enact a law by which a charter can be carried into effect that is granted by this House ? The speech of the hon. member for East Grey would lead us to suppose, in fact, he has made the solemn declaration, that he would wrest from these companies 'all the rights they have of crossing highways under the provisions of this section. That is a bold declaration to make. It may be one that will bring to him some influence in the rural districts but I am sure
I never made such a declaration.

I am glad to know I misunderstood the hon. gentleman and that he will not take such a position now. The hon. gentleman will lead us to suppose that this parliament has no powers. Surely, that is a peculiar contention. The parliament of Canada has the right to declare what are works for the general benefit of Canada. The parliament of Canada has the right to pass a general railway law, parliament has the right to incorporate railway companies and I must take this occasion for saying that I regret that hon. gentlemen opposite have so much to say about this charter jobbing and of people who are around grabbing up all these franchises. I cannot imagine what sort of men are conducting these affairs in the province of Ontario. We hear nothing of that kind in our province down by the sea and I cannot believe that the people who are organizing these companies are quite as bad as their friends over there paint them. If we have the right to enact a general railway law and if we have the right to charter railway companies must we not possess the right of saying that they can build their rail-

ways ? I would call the attention of lion, gentlemen to the present situation where it is proposed that a railway shall he built from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Suppose that we enacted here a provision by which that railway company, before it could cross a municipality, had to get the consent of that municipality.
No one has suggested that they should be prevented from crossing a municipality.
I do not want to put you wrong and you are not going to put me wrong.
Do not put up a man of straw,

If you are going to give a municipality this right for which the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is contending, then you must be logical and you cannot allow a railway to cross a municipality until they have obtained the consent of that municipality. That is the logical conclusion of what he said.
No.
The hon. gentleman repeated that.
We never contended that.	,

Would it be right or fair that a municipality could come in and say : Yon must not pass along a street of this municipality ? It may be the only possible place where they can pass through that municipality but the municipality will say :	No,
you cannot pass through, you will have to go around. Here is a provision which should be exercised only in extreme cases and we have appointed a tribunal to judge and determine as to when an extreme case arose and with such a provision I cannot see what my hon. friends have to complain of.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of the committee that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals shall have leave to withdraw his first amendment to section 184 that the following words be inserted ' incorporated after the passing of this Act' ?
Amendment withdrawn.

I would not waste the time of the committee by making any further observations regarding this subject if it were not for a statement or two made by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and by the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade). The hon. member for Annapolis has thought fit to read the hon. member for East Grey a lecture because he happened to be in this House years ago and did not object to a clause in the Railway
Act which was passed at that time, when so far as my knowledge goes he was not present. But he said these very same grievances existed in 1888 and that they existed even before confederation.
I did not use the word ' grievances.' Do not put words into my mouth.
I say these grievances exist to-day Why was it that the attention of parliament was not directed to the question then as it is to-day ?
You were here; we were not.
What is the matter with the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) ?
I say that you were here and we were not.

It is impossible for the hon. gentleman to keep quiet. It was because of, the fact that we had no electric railways and no street railways then in Canada. We had none of the troubles then that we have to-day.
No street railways in 1888 ?

I have answered the hon. member. I do not know whether he wants to be facetious or foolish. He can play either part to his heart's content. At the time when these discussions took place regarding provincial rights we had not street railways or electric railways to any great extent in Canada. They have grown up since that. At first when we had electric railways they were incorporated by the provinces, but since that it happened that the owners of these railway corporations came here for rights that had been denied by the provinces. They came here to secure rights that they could not get from the provinces and then they were taken out of the control of the provinces.
What electric railway in this Dominion has been incorporated by this parliament ?

I am going to address myself to the committee, not to the hon. member (Mr. Cowan) who seems so particularly anxious, whenever I am on my feet, to interrupt me. It is something that I have never done to him. I have had quite enough of it from .that source, and if I must say what will be very disagreeable, I will say it. I can tell the hon. gentleman that. At that time we. had very little trouble from this source, but when we began to take over these railway corporations and give them fhe powers that the federal parliament alone could give, strong objection was raised to it. Although the evil had not grown to the present extent, they were strenuously fought by members on both sides of this House,

and I regret to say that the contention of these gentlemen did not prevail. Of late years we have in two different ways invaded provincial rights ; one by taking over the charter rights conferred by {lie provinces and declaring them to be for the general advantage of Canada, and the other, by this parliament giving Acts of incorporation to roads that under the provisions of the British North America Act should he under the jurisdiction of the provinces. It is because of the growing tendency in this direction that there is a strong demand for the protection of provincial rights. The Minister of Railways said that if every one was like me it would be an unhappy day for the corporations. I did not propose to take away vested rights that were properly obtained, but I did say that I would have no hesitation in taking rights away from a corporation that were improperly obtained, and I repeat that statement on my full responsibility as a member of parliament. Suppose a man steals your horse and sells it to an innocent party, you have the right to take that horse back when you find it in the possession of the third party, and if these corporations become improperly possessed of public property, the public should have a right to claim them back. I have no respect for vested rights improperly acquired, and I am prepared at any time to restore these rights to their proper owners. I commend to the judgment of this House the amendment proposed by the member for Toronto, because it confirms to corporations the rights they have properly and legally secured.

The hon. gentleman is an old member of this House, and I am but a new member. Might I ask him if he was in the House supporting the government that proposed to wrest from the provinces the inland fisheries and the inland reserves?

That is foreign to the question we are discussing. It was declared by many legal authorities that we could not by the mere statement that a work was for the general advantage of Canada, take away provincial rights, and many of us allowed that question to be fought out in the courts. But there has since been a decision of the courts that we can take away these rights by such a declaration, and in view of that, we think it is time to stop it. I am consistent in my whole parliamentary career for I have always fought on the same lines as I am fighting to-night.

It must be amusing to the members of this House to hear the member for East Grey, that encyclopedia of ail parliamentary knowledge in his own judgment, saying for the first time in twenty-one years that he was now in favour of defending provincial rights. For the last twenty-one long years he has been wandering in the wilderness, and the greater part of that time
supporting a government that constantly invaded provincial rights.
Come back doctor.

I am not surprised that the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) should leave the Chamber. I rose to ask him whether he referred to street railways being incorporated by this parliament ? When he was speaking I asked him for the name of an electric railway that had been incorporated in the province of Ontario by this parliament, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule), shielding himself behind his rights, refused to answer, and stated that I was making an absurd interruption.
And then he runs away.

I rose in my place now for the purpose of addressing a few remarks to the member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the brave and gallant gentleman left the Chamber. For twenty-one years he was the enemy of provincial rights in this House, when men on this side who have grown grey in the service of their country were fighting the battles of provincial rights. For twenty-one years the hon. gentleman from East Grey was silent and dumb as an oyster in his shell, and voted every time against provincial rights in this House, but now at last he has suddenly found the light and he has become a champion of the provinces. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) saw fit to draw a comparison about a man stealing a horse, and I can only say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) reminded me of a story which comes'from the far off state of Kansas.
A new member of the legislature of that state after listening to a long speech void of either interest or merit arose, and in a nasal twang replied as follows ' Mr. Speaker, I have listened for the last hour or hour and a half to the hon. gentleman, not that what he said was worth listening to or the manner in which he said it particularly, interesting, but because I could not prevent my auricular organs from performing their natural functions within a reasonable distance of a noise of that description, and the longer I listened the more I was irresistibly driven to the conclusion that the honourable gentleman had started his mouth agoing and had then gone away and left it.
Oh, oh.

It seems to me that there are one or two important misapprehensions with regard to this clause. As I understand the question which has been raised just now, it is a very important one. There is no gentleman on this side of the House contending that a railway as distinguished from a street railway shall not be under the control of the board. I was call-

ing tlie attention of the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) to what I thought was a misapprehension on his part. I regard this as one of the most important propositions under the Bill, because it effects the jurisdiction of this House, the rights of this House, the rights of the provinces and the rights of the municipalities. As I understand it, no one on this side of the House objects to that part of the Bill which is the same as the old law. The hon. gentleman stated the old law correctly, as passed in 1888, I think, that a railway cannot be constructed along a highway of a municipality without an order from the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. That was the tribunal established to deal with such matters, after a very exhaustive inquiry by a commission presided over by Sir Alexander Galt, and it has remained the law until this Bill was introduced, under which we are shifting the authority to the hoard of railway commissioners. It is not contended on this side of the House that that should not be made the law. The amendment proposed relates entirely to street railways. My hon. friend from Annapolis accused somebody of putting up men of straw to knock them down, and I think he put up one without intending to do so. Possibly he misunderstood the hon. gentleman on this side of the House, because I can assure him that my hon. friends on this side, those who are old members, from the care and trouble that many of them have taken in discussing this Bill, are most anxious to have a proper Bill.
What does the hon. gentleman want ? I have been listening for two hours and a half to try to find out what hon. gentlemen opposite are driving at.

I doubt if I have spoken an hour in the House during this session or two hours during the last session. I want to assure the minister that my hon. friends on this side of the House are discussing the Bill with a desire to improve it. They may be wrong in some instances, and I am free to say that with some of their contentions I have disagreed ; and I may disagree with them in regard to some other matters. The difficulty seems to arise from the powers to be exercised by railways proper as contra-distinguished from street railways. The hon. member for Annapolis seemed to misunderstand that.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to interject a remark ? I am sure I take very great pleasure in listening to anything the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) says on any question pertaining to railways. I know that his sole desire in discussing this Bill is to make it as good an Act as he possibly can ; and I believe that every hon. gentleman on this side of the House will agree with me in that. But what I stated was that this Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
parliament has not yet incorporated a street railway company, as far as I know. It is a question which will have to be determined by this, parliament, whether it will incorporate street railways or not. But if this parliament does in its wisdom see lit to incorporate street railways, then I submit that the control of these railways and the regulating of their running and crossing must be under this board. I submit to the hon. gentleman if that is not a fair proposition.
I quite admit that ; but the hon. member for Annapolis went further than that. He charged gentlemen cn this side of the House
Not the present speaker.

If I understood the ton. gentleman rightly, he charged the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) with having been in the House when a law was passed by the Conservative government, and now going back on it and objecting to it. The hon. member for East Grey is not objecting to it any more than he did when it was passed. The hon. member for East Grey has always held what I called radical opinions on this subject, and to my certain recollection he opposed his own party at different times in connection with that Act. But it was the law, and we on this side of the House are not objecting to it. It is satisfactory that both sides of the House can concur thus far. The hon. gentleman lor West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), who spoke so ably and so strongly about municipal rights, did not object to the railway commission having control in Toronto or outside of it over railways proper, but he does object strongly to it having control over street railways. I go with the hon. member for East Grey this far. When the Act was passed in 18S8, we hardly heard anything about street railways. This country has progressed, however, and electric railways have grown up rapidly and have become important, without the question as to what jurisdiction wTe do exercise or should exercise over them having been raised. But that has become a very important question, and I am bound to say for myself, that for some time I was not impressed as much as I have been lately, since the discussion of this Bill has arisen, as to the exercise of the power of declaring the work to be for the general advantage of Canada. I understand that under the constitution we have power to do that if we see fit. I believe that the British North America Act gives that power to us absolutely, trusting to this House not to exercise it improperly ; because under our constitution, as I understand it, the right of eminent domain is relegated largely to this parliament, to the extent that wTe have at least concurrent jurisdiction with the provinces on many of these questions, and this is said to be one of them. I do not under-

stand that that is challenged on either side of the House. This question of street railways has become important, particularly in the larger towns of Ontario, and we must pay attention to it and investigate it. The provincial legislature has sent a memorial to this House, finding fault with the manner in which we have seemed to exercise that important power. Now, 1 am one of those who are not willing to abnegate one title of our power. At the same time, when we have a discretionary power, of course we must be careful and reasonable in exercising it. This has become an important question, and I think both sides of the House are willing to consider it, and I have no doubt that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has been troubled a good deal in the preparation of this new Act, which had to do two important things. One is the establishment of a railway commission and the other defining the powers and jurisdiction of that commission, particularly with regard to electric railways.
This question of electric tramways and their relations with the municipalities is a difficult one for to deal with and possibly may . require to be dealt with by a general Act applying especially to them alone. Evidently the hon. minister is not disposed to go as far in excluding electric tramways from municipalities without their first obtaining the consent of these municipalities as hon. gentlemen on this side desire, and we shall therefore have to be more careful when special Acts come up to see that the rights of the municipalities are in each case protected, but there is no doubt that there must be some tribunal to decide disputes between these companies and the municipalities in cases where the companies have been incorporated by this parliament. That tribunal must necessarily be the railway commission. Such disputes have frequently come before the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, and I have never known a case in which the municipality was not content to abide by its decision. There is no doubt a great deal in the contention that these tramways should be left exclusively within the jurisdiction of the local authorities, and the fact that the hon. minister is not bringing in a general measure to deal with them leads me to believe that he is disposed to take that view himself, but of course we cannot abrogate entirely our right to interfere. I am in accord with the hon. minister in protecting the rights that we have granted, but I am sorry that he could not go the length in protecting the municipalities desired on this side of the House.

I would like the hon. gentleman to answer the question I put to him. I am asking for information only. Suppose this parliament does incorporate an electric tramway, does he not think that that tramway should come under the operation of the General Railway Act of Canada ?

I am sorry that the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) has left the Chamber, as 1 was anxious to enlighten him with regard to the question he put some time ago. That hon. gentleman however seldom favours us with his presence for any length of time, but contents himself with coming in now and then and by his interruptions seeking to turn our parliamentary proceedings into a farce. He undertook to show his superior knowledge to mine by pointing out that the electric railways were not dealt with in this Bill at all, and he did not give me a chance to set him right. Why, we have taken up nearly the whole day in discussing an amendment of the hon. Minister of Railways which deals exclusively with electric companies, and further let me draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to sections 5 and 1 which also deal with electric companies. And section 7, as I have said, brings all these electric railways within the scope of these provisions. Perhaps some hon. gentleman will inform the hon. member for South Essex that when he comes in to interrupt legislation with very doubtful contributions to the debates of the House-perhaps, in kindness to me, they will inform him-that he should be more careful in his interruptions in the future and should learn something of what he intends to talk about. The hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) sneers at us ont this side as champions of provincial rights. I do not know whether he means by that that he is a better champion of provincial rights than we are. I assume that he is not going to interfere with provincial rights improperly. And I would point out to him what he would have known had he been attending to his duty Sere for the past week or two. I pointed it out to the Minister of Railways. The general Railway Act of Ontario, the Electric Railway Act, and the Street Railway Act, of that province, all dealing with the subject here touched upon contain provisions by which it is expressly enacted that no railway shall pass upon or along any highway, but may only cross the same, without the consent of the municipality. If the hon. member for Annapolis wants to have the legislation of this parliament directly in conflict with that of the largest province of the Dominion-I do not pretend to say whether the legislation of his own province is the same in this respect as that of Ontario, though I think it likely that it is- if he wants the legislation of this House to be directly in conflict with that of the largest province on a question that has been piiima facie delegated to the provinces, the right to control the highways, of course, the hon. gentleman must be left to his choice. Under the circumstances, I need not weary the House longer with the discussion of the argument of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade). I wish to impress upon the minister the absolute inconsistency of the law as he pro-

poses to leave it sin saying that the electric railways shall not be permitted to deal with the board without the consent of the municipalities, so far as cities and towns are concerned, but that that consent shall not be required in the villages and townships. And I would desire, notwithstanding what the minister said a little while ago and notwithstanding the insinuation he made (and which may have included me) to urge this point once more upon him. The hon. minister insinuated that we on this side were talking too much, and that hon. members on his own side accomplished more by seeing him privately with regard to proposed amendments. I do not think it is our duty to go to the hon. minister privately to ask if he will agree to have legislation amended. I think it was better to bring the matter before the House and get the combined wisdom of the two hundred and fourteen members of this Chamber upon our arguments, and not attempt ' Star ' chamber legislation in regard to such an important Act as this is. I doubt whether good would be accomplished by what the hon. minister thinks ought to be done, and I think it is more charitable to him and better for the Dominion that we should assume that in speaking as he did about us and about hon. gentlemen on his own side he was only joking, for lie has made no amendments in the interest of the people that did not come from this side of the House.

I am going to ask that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. But, before doing so, I wish to make an observation. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) and the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), I think, were present when this subject was under discussion before. They urged very strongly-I know the hon. member for Lincoln did at least-what the hon. member for Halton is now advocating. That point was thoroughly discussed. I think it is only a fair claim I am making upon the committee when I say that, when we have had an exhaustive discussion upon any one question, and a full opportunity to consider it, and when that question has been disposed of, it is not entirely reasonable to present the same arguments again and ask to have the subject reconsidered. My hon. friend, I think, coincided with the view I then stated that, so far as electric railways are concerned, after very careful consideration I concluded that we might properly make provisions that they should not be allowed to operate in any city or incorporated town unless dnth the consent of the municipal authority.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think I heard all that the hon. gentleman said on that subject. I know he said it would make it apply to cities and towns. But I have never yet been able to get him to state a reason for not making it apply to incorporated villages and rural municipalities.

I think I must have stated my reasons; I must have replied to the hon. gentleman's question. I did not think it desirable to give to all municipalities the same control that we were giving to the councils of towns and cities. We were giving them this power without any appeal at all. The flat or decision of the municipal council of a city or incorporated town is made final. I can well understand that in the ease of a populous centre, the streets ought not to be used except under some such conditions as we have laid down here. But when it comes to country districts, many of them sparsely settled, the case is different. It may be a great convenience to people living at long distances apart to have a street railway to facilitate communication, and I do not think it would be reasonable or proper that any one of these townships through which a railway was seeking to have the privilege of running should have the power to hold up the street railway company. I think that that would be an extreme power to give without any right of appeal. That is my reason, and I still think the reason is a sufficient one. Hon. members are debating this question as though we were incorporating electric railways between towns and cities in vast numbers. We are not doing anything of the sort, and I hope we are not going to. As I said before, I shall lend my voice as far as I can to refuse charters to these purely local companies wherever they come from.
I do not think we should pass such charters. There are very few instances where such incorporations have been granted. I think it would be difficult to name half a dozen in Ontario, and I do not know of any in the eastern provinces. There may be one or two in the province of Quebec.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There are several in the province of Ontario. There is one that was from Port Perry to the Georgian bay, to Kincardine, Meaford, Owen Sound, South Lambton and Durham. There is another radial railway around the city of Guelph, another that extends to Galt and Preston. These are all under Dominion charters.

I think the hon. gentleman is not up to my limit yet, and probably he has named all he can think of. Now these people ought to have gone to the provincial legislature. I would send them there. Therefore, I hope the committee will see its way to allow this clause to pass as a proposed amendment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would ask the minister why he excludes villages, though many incorporated villages are larger than some incorporated towns ?

An incorporated village might cover a largo area, and yet have a sparse

population, a much less population than an incorporated town.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I rise to dispute a statement that has been frequently made, that this parliament has never granted any electric railway charters.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS ANI) CANALS. Surely the hon. gentleman is not quoting me as having said that ?

No, it was the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade), and I think the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan), who stated that frequently to-night. I want to point out that as far back as 1899 this parliament granted a charter to the Montreal Island Belt Line Railway, and to change its name to the Montreal Terminal Railway Company. In this charter hon. gentlemen will find these words :	' may be
operated by electricity only.' So here is an electric railway charter, notwithstanding the statement made by these hon. gentlemen. I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that more lines of railway are being constructed in this country that use electricity and other motive powers than steam, and it is their intention to carry freight and passengers, and to interchange freight and passengers with railways that are under the General Railway Act of Canada. The minister has already conceded legislation in his Bill to meet the case I have quoted ; therefore, I say lion, gentlemen on this side of the House are quite justified in using the language they did with regard to electric railway lines.

I trust the minister will pardon me for pressing my amendment. I said, when on my feet before, that I had been requested to ask the minister to extend the same favour to minor municipalities as had been extended in this section to cities and incorporated towns. I will read a resolution passed at a meeting held in the town of Oakville, in the county I have the honour to represent, on the 24th of June last:
Moved, by Colonel Kerns, reeve of Burlington, seconded by Mr. Bryans, reeve of Etobicoke, that the amendment of the honourable the Minister of Railways not allowing electric railways to enter upon any street or highway in any city or incorporated town be extended to include all municipalities.
That is the request I referred to. Therefore, I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Blain, that section 184 as amended be further amended by adding after the word ' town ' where it occurs in said amendment, the words ' or other municipality.'

The hon. member evidently is under the impression that all any of these companies would have to do would be to go to the Board of Railway Commissioners and they would get permission to enter upon
the streets of municipalities. Now that is contrary to all experience. They do not get this permission except in cases which are made abundantly clear. If the people in any locality petition against it, 1 do not think there is any board of railway commissioners that would give permission to a railway company to enter upon the streets of a municipality unless it were very necessary that such permission should he granted.
