Take for instance, a case where a street railway or an electric railway traversed through several rural townships or villages. Supposing that there was one municipality at one end which was in favour of granting the company this power and petitioned for it, and supposing that at the other end another municipality was also in favour of giving this permission to the company, but that between these two was a third municipality which was opposed, which for some reason or other declined to fall into line with the other two, and said : We don't want this tramway running upon our streets, we won't give them permission. Would it be right that one township or one village should be able to hold up the whole enterprise ? If an instance of this kind occurred, and the law was changed, as the hon. gentleman suggests, there would be no remedy ; if it occurred under the existing provisions of our Bill, there would be a remedy, because they could go to the board and show the board what the difficulty was, and the board would have the power to decide the question. Now in ail these cases there ought to be some controlling power, some independent tribunal, which would consider such a difficulty from an independent standpoint and pass upon it. I do not think it would be advisable to carry this clause, and, therefore, I hope the hon. gentleman will not press it. If he does I will have to ask the committee not to accept it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The case I have in my mind is one where I am sure the municipalities want the electric railway that will ask for a charter to-morrow night but they do not want the electric railway to run along the streets or highways, at any rate, without their having something to say as to the conditions on which they should do so.
Put that in the Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The very fact that the Bill, as we have it now, makes provision that the consent of a city or incorporated town must be obtained and that no reference whatever is made to a township or village corporation to my mind would lead to the conclusion that they would not have the right to make any remonstrance to the board before the board adjudicated upon the matter although the hon. minister has told us that the board would not be likely to deal with it until they had heard from the municipalities.
The Railway Committee of the Privy Council has never dealt with such a case without hearing from the municipalities.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
This is possible, but I dare say that under the law as it existed before, there was no such distinction between an incorporated town and an incorporated village. Here there is such a distinction. We are to have a board on which certain rights and powers are conferred by the statute. It may well say to one : We will listen to you, and to the other : We are not called upon to listen to you. I would like to take the sense of the committee on that resolution, because I know the intense feeling that prevails in my county in reference to this very matter, and I would not be doing my duty did I not urge upon the hon. minister to grant us the same rights as have been accorded to the city of Toronto and accorded to a small town in my own county. I refer to the town of Oakville.
The MINISTER OF RAILW^xS AND CANALS. We had better strike them all out probably.
I am quite satisfied.

While I do not pretend to talk about railway matters, I must call the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to an incident that occurred in the county of Peel when I was a member of the county council. An electric railway company came to the county council and asked for liberty to run its track along a certain part of the highway, but the council flatly refused because it was thought that accidents would result to farmers with their horses and cattle on the highway if street cars were allowed to be run there. The county council took the view that if the electric railway were a paying affair the promoters should be compelled to buy their right of way the same as any other railway company. * It is very annoying to farmers, particularly with young horses, to go out on the highway and meet an electric railway ear. I think that the rights of rural municipalities should be recognized in this matter as well as those of cities. If an electric railway is a paying enterprise the company should be compelled to buy their right of way in the direction which they wish to go. The county of Peel absolutely refused to grant this company running rights over a certain road from Toronto to Oakville. I know that in our section of the country the people are opposed to allowing electric railways to be established on the highways, because of the difficulty they have with young horses. Street ears can be controlled on the road and no damage will be done to them, but if their operation on the highways is legalized by legislation they have a right to run Mr. HENDERSON.
there and in the event of damage being done to people in vehicles drawn by horses which are not manageable, the injured parties have no redress. I think the rights of municipalities should be guarded as well as those of cities and towns.
Progress reported.

Some resolutions reported.

Wednesday, July 8, 1903.']

In the legislation which has passed this House respecting railway mail clerks, provision has been made to increase the salaries of these officials. Is it the intention of the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) to provide for any increase in the salaries of railway transfer agents ? These are men who are connected with the railway mail service and who transfer the mails from train to train at divisional points and elsewhere. I have been asked to put that question to the Postmaster General.
The Act, passed last session, makes provision for increases in the salaries of the railway mail transfer agents.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speechtext: Does not that say ' hereafter appointed ' ?
It also contains a provision allowing them during the six months to come in under the provisions of the Act.
I have been asked if it is the intention to increase the salaries of those officials Who handle the mails at the different divisional points of the railway.
They will come in under the Bill at present before the Senate.
They are provided for ?
Yes.

There are post office clerks who are now sent out on a line to assist the railway mail clerks for the purpose of accelerating the delivery of letters by the first delivery. They practically do the work of the railway mail clerks and they are liable to the same risks, but they are not provided for. Is it the intention of the Postmaster General to grant these gentlemen mileage ?
These are post office clerks and they are eligible for the promotions that the Bill which has passed this House contemplates.
Their occupation when engaged on railway service is more hazardous than when employed in the post office.
No doubt.

Is it not fair that these gentlemen should have mileage for the time they are on duty on the trains', as well as the railway mail clerks V The POSTMASTER GENERAL. I do not think so. They are not fully responsible like railway mail clerks and they only make a run for a short distance. They retain their status as post office clerks.
Would the Postmaster General tell the House what progress has been made towards the introduction of rural mail delivery.

I have not yet reached a conclusion upon that subject. I have had it looked into by the officers to a considerable extent, but it is a very large and serious question indeed. Some very wild statements have been made from time to time as to its supposed paying character, but I do not know that they are founded on fact. The| United States Post Office Department is going through an ordeal just now over it. They voted millions upon millions for the service, and the first reports made by their officers seemed to indicate that it was remunerative. It now turns out that a number of the high officials responsible for that service are under criminal indictment for frauds of vafious kinds, and I am inclined to think! that their reports in regard to the service have not been reliable. Questions are now engaging the attention of the criminal courts of the United States and we are not warranted up to this moment in taking the records of the United States in this respect as a safe guide. It is estimated that it will cost the United States some $25,000,000 to establish a system of even a limited character. We should approach that matter with very great care in order not to make mistakes. Should the system be established in Canada, although we might in the first instance throw safeguards around it yet, it might naturally lead us into a very serious financial problem. I have not been able to reach a conclusion in favour of the important step of establishing a. rural mail delivery in Canada. I do not wish to take any attitude against! ,jt, and my present opinion is that it is wise to defer reaching a conclusion until the system has been longer on trial in the United States.

I do not dispute the proposition of the Postmaster General in any way, but I would like to ask him whether he has considered the carrying on of an experiment in the matter without adopting any policy in reference to rural mail delivery ? Would it not be possible for him to, select some limited section of the country and make an experiment with regard to it V Has the hon. gentleman made any inquiry into tliis svstem outside of the examination of the United States postal records ? I know that there is a strong feeling among a considerable portion of the rural community that they would like to have this service,
and they have asked their representatives to urge it upon the Post Office Department, that if they can undertake the service without any unjustifiable expense the Post Office Department should do so as soon as possible.

In reply to the hon. gentleman's inquiry as to whether the department has any data other than the official postal records, I have to say that some of the officers of the Post Office Department have visited the actual routes traversed by some of the rural mail-carriers and have informed themselves as accurately as possible, from actual observation of the work, as to the extent of the mail matter which is being carried, and they report the greatest discrepancy between the number of pieces of mail matter carried on those occasions by the couriers and the official returns of the same trips. Speaking from memory, I believe that in one instance tlie official return of the number of letters supposed to be carried on a certain route was near 500, while by actual count by one of my officers, the number was forty-eight or thereabouts, which shows how unreliable the official report was in that instance. I am not in a position to characterize all the reports in the same way-far from it; I would not be warranted in doing that. But that was the result of the count in that instance, and my officer was in actual communication with the couriers themselves. As to experimenting, that would be the only safe way to proceed ; but even in that case it would be necessary to select representative routes and districts and to provide proper safeguards. I suggested to one of the officers who has been studying the matter particularly, to endeavour to devise a set of regulations or specifications which would be safe to follow in a test of that kind. As yet he has not been able to do so. Probably this fall the officers will make another trip and investigate further. We have investigated in many states almost from the Atlantic to west of Detroit, in order that we may reach safe conclusions. I can only say that it is a subject of such importance that it can only be approached after the fullest investigation. I should rejoice if during my tenure as Postmaster General I could have the honour of inaugurating a system which is apparently of such great convenience to the rural people, but I would not wish, for the sake of a personal pleasure and satisfaction, to take a step that might result disastrously to the country.

The bags are collected at different centres, and have to be taken to the repair shops, whether at Aurrra or at any

other place. I am not aware why Aurora, though it may be a small place, is not entitled to some consideration. St. John gets its attention from the government in many ways. It is a seaport town and has been equipped with public works at a very large expense. While the cities of this Dominion have benefited by government expenditure, very little is done in the rural constituencies in the way of public works, and they are therefore entitled to some attention in a matter of this kind. At all events the country has got good value for the work done.

The Postmaster General is to be congratulated on his frankness if on nothing else. He admits that no tenders are called for for this large amount of supplies-it runs up into the thousands of dollars-though there is every reason to believe that if public competition were invited prices would be lessened very considerably. I do not know the rate of wages paid to the workmen engaged in repairing under the old government. At first, on taking office I did not inquire as to the wages being paid by the employer. Subsequently, when increasing the allowance the chief object I had in view was to enable the employer to pay a fair wage, I do not know whether there is an affidavit of the wages paid on these small jobs. But an affidavit is required in the case of the manufacturers making the bags. Who fixes the minimum rate ? Is this where the fairwage officer gets his work in ? Who determines in the various localities what should be the minimum wage ?

The only contract of this kind, I think, is in the city of Toronto, except a very small contract made with Mr. Willis, of Aurora. The chief contract is for the manufacture of the ordinary mail bags that are sent everywhere with His Majesty's mails. A large number are used per annum, and the contract w&s a very substantial one. That was let by tender to the Ottawa Supply Company. That contract was made long prior to the establishment of a Labour Department, or thei appointment of a fair wage officer. I think I am correct in saying that it was let in the year 1898. On that occasion I myself made inquiries of certain representatives of labour in the city of, Ottawa, ana submitted to them the question what would be a fair wage to be paid by the contractor for the manufacture

of these mail bags. The persons to whom I applied for information called a meeting of the representative work people in this city who were doing the kind of work involved in making these mail bags, and they made a report to me, setting forth what in their opinion was a fair prevailing wage in the city of Ottawa, and that wage was adopted in connection with the contract.
What contracts have been let since then ?

The contract only ran out a few months ago, and it has recently been relet, I do not know whether it is yet signed. I think it is only a week or two since the deputy informed me of the result of the tenders. I have no doubt he has adopted the same method, but he would not have to take the same trouble. But I have no doubt the same principle is applied, and that the minimum wage is set forth in the contract.
Are these the only two contracts ?
I said there is a small contract for bags let to Willis & Sons, of Aurora. But .it is a trifling one, the Auditor General's Report will show it.

I find that this last year this gentleman Mr. Winter, received $74 simply for the cartage of these old mail bags back and forward to the place where the repairs were made. It seems to me a most exorbitant sum to pay a man for doing a little carting. The committee will be astonished to know that Mr. Winter gets $74 when it is by grace of the member of his county, the Postmaster General, but when Mr. Winter has to enter into open competition to carry ordinary mail bags back and forth from the train, he is pleased to make twenty-four trips a week, four trips every day in the year, except Sundays, for the sum of $120. I think that other men throughout the country who are forced to go into public competition to perform mail courier service at low rates, will be astonished to find that a constituent and a strong political supporter of the Postmaster General is treated in this most kindly manner.

There is a little difference in the task of carrying a small quantity of mail matter to and from the station and carrying wagon loads of bags, which involves a good deal of labour and perhaps more appliances. The bags are bulky, and a man would have to have a wagon ana horse, and to handle and rehandle the bags. That is different from merely going to the station for a small amount of mail matter.

I would like to ask the Postmaster General this question. I find by reference to the report of 1900 that a firm called the Ottawa Supply Company furnished $11,630 worth of supplies, that in the year 1901 they furnished $16,500 worth of supplies and that last year they supplied $15,338 worth. May I ask if these supplies were furnished under public competition, and moreover, who the Ottawa Supply Company are ? I have searched the directory and they seem to have no place of business.

I do not know the personnel of the Ottawa Supply Company, and I never did know. I know they tendered recently again and lost the contract. As to whether these contracts were made by public tender or not, I am not able to say, but I think tenders were invited. I can recollect having a considerable number of tenders submitted to me by the superintendent of the stores branch.
There was| a fair system of tendering and *the -work was obtained at fair prices, at much more advantageous prices than those paid under the former administration.
Do I understand the hon. minister to say that tenders were not called for but that the goods were supplied at what the department considered fair prices ?
I did not make such a statement.
Were public tenders invited, and if so was the Ottawa Supply Company the lowest tenderer for this large amount ?

Speaking from memory only, while tenders were not publicly invited, tenders were invited by circular from reliable persons and the contract was awarded in competition and the Ottawa Supply Company obtained the contract as the lowest tenderer. That is my recollection, and I am sure it is the case, because I can recall the circumstances of the superintendent having extended the tenders in the book. I think the deputy Informed me who was the successful tenderer, but at an earlier stage I took a more detailed part in the work of the department. Under the contract with the Ottawa Supply Company the cost of mail bags was less and materially less than under the system in force when I took office.

I must protest against this way of conducting business in the hon. gentleman's department. I think it is utterly unfair that the hon. Postmaster General should discriminate in the way he does. I do not think that is a businesslike proposition and I say there should be open, honest, fair competition when such a large amount as $42,000 worth is to be purchased. Another item is the Crown Tailoring Company, Toronto, $1,801. Another is Caldwell, Boyd & Co., Lanark, material for letter-carriers' uniforms, 1,249 yards, at $1.75, and 140 yards, at $1.15, making a total of $2,347. There are three items, page S-43, making a total of about $6,500. Will the minister say whether tenders were asked for these supplies. While I am on my feet, I would like the minister to tell us whether it is the policy of his department in the purchasing of supplies, to ask for tenders, and what proportion of the supplies purchased year by year are purchased under tender, that splendid system which the hon. minister advocated when in opposition, and which indeed was one of the planks of the platform of his party. What I want to know is whether the hon. gentleman has forgotten all that, or whether he is applying what he advocated in opposition to the purchase of supplies for his department ?

The hon. gentleman has referred me to page S-43 of the Auditor General's Report, and the first name I find there is that of the American Bank Note Company, which received the sum of $23,305 for printing postage stamps, &c. The contract was let about the year 1897. There was at that time another company here doing business, the British American Bank Note Company, and the government invited tenders from these two companies, and awarded the contract to the American Bank Note Company. That contract has, I think, expired and been renewed. I am not aware of there being many persons from whom to invite to tender for that class of work. The tender was awarded. As a result of that tendering, the Minister of Finance explained to the House that the government had effected a saving of something like $150,000 or $160,000. As to

the Crown Tailoring Company's contract, that was obtained after tenders were invited by circular
From whom ?

I have not got a list of the names. The contract was awarded as a result of that system of tendering, which, in the case of goods of that kind, I think is quite a proper system. As to Bailey, his supplies were ink, &c., and I do not know whether tenders were called for or not. He supplies a number of articles, letter boxes, locks, pens, ink, and other small items.	.
Where does the hon. the minister get his letter boxes ?
Some are made in Aurora.
They are very badly made.
Which ones ?
The boxes that open with keys. In Lindsay they are not fit to use.

These were put in when the public building was erected, and they were put in by my predecessors, but there have been great improvements of later years in the design of letter-boxes, and I do not think that it will be said that the lock letter-boxes now are not good. The last letter-boxes put in were in connection with station C in Toronto. I think the design is a credit to the company, and a great advantage to the country.
Has the hon. gentleman found the letter from Mr. Million that he promised to bring ?
No.
Where were the postal bags made ?
At the corner of Lyon and Sparks street.
That is at the Butler House-a hotel.
There are several corners.
The other one is a public market.
He may not have meant literally on the corner. The factory is over a store called the Stratton grocery store, where these bags are made.
The hon. minister has not told us whether the $16,000 of supplies got from the Ottawa Supply Company were got by tender.

The contract was let several years ago, and
tenders were invited from a number of qualified persons, and the invitations were not confined to our friends. I think that we invited tenders from the people who had been supplying the late government. There was good competition, and the prices were materially less than previously.
What were the prices paid previously?
I cannot say, but I remember my superintendent telling me that there was a very material reduction.	,
Were all those invited to tender on the patronage list ?
I do not think so.
What is the practice. Are circulars sent only to persons who are lucky enough to be on the patronage list ?

I do not know whether there is any regular practice prevailing. In my department l endeavour to see that circulars are sent to competent men. We do not always get satisfactory results from advertising for tenders for certain classes of goods. For example, suppose you advertise for clothing, you may adopt a very strict specification and not get satisfactory results, as to the character and material and so on. If the contract is let very low and the contractor is not going to make money, he will endeavour to save himself by furnishing inferior goods. That is one of the chief drawbacks of the tender system. It is found in many instances wiser to invite tenders from persons of recognized standing in the trade.
How do they get on the patronage list ?
If the hon. gentleman has any worthy manufacturer he desires to have put on the patronage list, all he has to do is to send to some minister the name of that person.
Suppose I were to send some one to the hon. gentleman, would he put him on the list ?
I dare say I would, if the hon. gentleman will let this item through.

The hon. minister has not answered two of the questions I put him. I see the firm of Geo. Bailey & Company, of Ottawa, was paid $3,916.15 ; Caldwell Boyd & Company, Lanark, $2,347.99, and Pritchard, Andrews & Company, of Ottawa, $7,905.08. Were tenders asked for in these cases ?

The prices paid Pritchard, Andrews & Company for the miscellaneous articles purchased

from them are the regular set prices. I do not see how we could possibly have invited tenders, because the articles purchased are small matters of a great variety, and but few of each description. For instance, they comprise four numbering machines, brass buttons, cast iron plates for letter-boxes, steel stamp with crown, and a lot of other miscellaneous articles. With reference to the scales, I think tenders were invited. There are not very many scale makers in Canada, but notices were sent to Messrs. Gurney & Company, of Hamilton, some firm in Montreal and Pritchard, Andrews & Company, here, and perl'aps others. The scales required for the post office must be well made, because they must do delicate weighing. Therefore, it would not do to accept tenders except from makers who are known to be able to make scales of the quality required by the department. My impression is that Pritchard, Andrews & Company have made a specialty of manufacturing these post office scales for many years. They supplied the department long before I came into office, as hon. gentlemen can see by turning up the public accounts of former years. I am under the impression-still, I may be doing them an injustice -that we cannot even claim them as our political friends.
I rather differ with the hon. minister as to an account of $7,900 as being so small that it is not worth-
I did not say that.
I stand corrected. Do I understand the hon. minister to say that the account of the Pritchard and Andrews Company consisted of such items as could not well be tendered for ?
Some of them.

I see one item of 927 stamps at $3.75. That I should look upon as an order worth tendering for if the policy of the department is to ask for tenders. I would not extend my remarks further on that point, but would just ask the hon. minister to say generally whether it is the policy of the department to ask for tenders for the supply of such articles as we have been discussing to-night ?
There are some classes of articles which are properly subjects for tenders, and some that cannot be made so. Take the account of the Pritchard and Andrews Company. It is a pity to go into details-
I do not ask the hon. gentleman to do that.

The hon. gentleman speaks of an account amounting to $7,905.08, and asks whether I do Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
not think that it would be made a subject for tender, I hardly think the question suggests a proper answer. The subject matter of the account, I think, would determine the answer much better than the amount. Here are some of the items in this account: Bate's numbering machine (5 wheels) 4 at $17.50-that is a little machine for paging-brass crown seals, 103 at 35 cents- that is something in connection with the coat of arms on the mail bags-Brass buttons, cleaned and burnished, 130 gross at 75 cents; cast iron plates for letter boxes, 10 at 50 cents; dated stamps, 927 at $3.75-
How about that item ?

These people have been manufacturing these dated stamps for many years and have been recognized suppliers of the government. They are reliable people, and there is some nicety required in the manufacture of date stamps and they have become experts in that branch. Therefore, it is in the public interest that they should be allowed to continue the furnishing of these supplies. They are highly respectable people and reliable; and it is not the practice of the department, in supplies of that kind to have them made here and there. There is uniformity to be considered. Therefore, the custom has been to order from them. If there were a change of the government, I am sure our successors would do as we have done; we are following exactly in the footsteps of our predecessors.
A pretty safe thing to do.

I agree that it would not be possible to invite tenders for many of the items the hon. gentleman has referred to. We do not contend that it is possible to have tenders where the department requires one or two letter boxes, or wishes to have brass buttons burnished. But what I would like from the minister is an answer in a general way. Would he say whether it is the general policy of the department to call for tenders in the purchase of supplies. I see on two pages of the Auditor General's Report accounts for supplies and in all they amount to about $150,000. Is it the policy of the department to call for tenders in these large items or not ?

The policy of the v department is to obtain supplies with reasonable competition where the goods are of a nature to be tendered for. In pursuance of that policy, tenders are invited for the furnishing of postage Stamps. I find one extension of this account amounts to $23,305. Then the next item is $3,309, dead letter stamps, &c. These are also furnished by the company under contract. Post cards, &c., $18,801. These goods have been also obtained in the same way. Letter cards, $2,104. Post bands, $1,878. There are about $50,000 worth of goods supplied by the American Bank Note Company as a result of tenders in the manner I have explained. The Crown Tailoring Company, Toronto, furnished goods to the value of $1,801, obtained by tender.
Who is the Crown Tailoring Company ?
The only person whose name I know is George Anderson.
A Liberal candidate of East Toronto.
I think so. His place of business is on Front street in the city of Toronto. I think the contract with Sanford & Co., of Hamilton, for uniforms, was also a result of tenders.

Would it be fair to the hon. gentleman to state the case in this way : In no case does his department ask for public competition except in the narrow form of selecting business houses of good standing, and asking tenders from these ? But in no case does he ask for tenders by public competition, allowing every person to tender.
Not for supplies.

I understood the minister to say that he asks for tenders from those who are in the business of manufacturing the articles he wants, ouly from reliable firms. I would like to know how he can make that statement insofar as the Ottawa Supply Company are concerned. This supply company, I am informed, is composed of Stratton Bros., who run a little grocery store on a street in the outskirts of the city, and with them was an employee of the government who was supposed to manipulate this deal. Now this firm simply dickered out this contract. I am satisfied that the minister could have purchased by tender and public competition this $42,000 worth of goods supplied during three years, for much less than he paid these gentlemen. I am satisfied the minister would never have acted in that way if he were buying goods for his own use. In this instance, and in the instance of the Crown Tailoring
Company, he gave contracts to persons who are not in the business at all. He has admitted that he has been giving out large contracts, some $42,000 worth, to parties who were not in the business and never were, and had no means of manufacturing the goods they supplied. Now this Ottawa Supply Company are down here in addition for making wooden boxes. Now, they cannot manufacture wooden boxes in an upstairs place over a grocery store. They furnished 3,500 wooden boxes, which could have been purchased from some box factory much cheaper than from the Ottawa Supply Company. I would like to ask the minister who compose this Canadian Fostal Supply Company, in Montreal, who, for the rent of two mail marking machines, are paid $200. Would the miiiister state in what way these machines are used, and has the same company a contract for other cities ?

The hon. gentleman says that tenders were invited from persons who were not in the business, in the case of the Crown Tailoring Company of Toronto, and the Ottawa Supply Company. In regard to the Crown Tailoring Company, he is entirely in error. I never knew anything about the Ottawa Supply Company! But I do know that the place of business of the Crown Tailoring Company is situated on Front street, in Toronto, and the company is largely engaged in business. The hon. gentleman will find that store a short distance west of Yonge street, between that and York street. There is a very large establishment with the name of the Crown Tailoring Company. That I believe to be the headquarters of the company that has supplied the goods in question here. The hon. gentleman is in error when he says that they were not in the trade.
How about the Ottawa Supply Company ?
I have discussed that. The hon. gentleman was not here when we discussed that.
Yes. I was here.

Then the hon. gentleman should know all about it. We made a contract with the Ottawa Supply Company as a result of fair competition with very substantial manufacturers of this city who were proper persons to supply bags. As a result of that competition this Ottawa Supply Company, being the lowest tenderers, obtained the contract and they have delivered the goods to us in accordance to the specifications and of good quality at much lower prices than were being paid under my predecessors at the time of the change of government. When their contract expired recently, tenders were again invited, they tendered and they lost the contract. Some other person got it. I do not know who.
Does the hon. gentleman know who has the contract now ?
I have lust said that I do not know. It is only within the last month the deputy told me the result of the tendering.
Are these public tenders ?
I have explained all that several times.
Just in regard to that point.

I have said that we invited tenders from reliable persons but not by advertisement. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid, Grenville) asked me about this account.
Canadian Postal Supply Company, Montreal, rent of two mail marking machines, twelve months, $400.
This is an invention for obliterating stamps on letters and it is a very rapid working machine. I do not know by whom it was invented but the firm of Dolphin & Hay in the United States supplied this machine to the United States government and we have had several of them installed in different offices throughout Canada. I think there are two in Montreal.
There are six in Montreal.

There is one in Ottawa, two in Toronto, and there are some elsewhere. They do very rapid work and they are the best stamp cancelling machines up to date. I do not know anything about a company under the name of the Canadian Postal Supply Company. We made our arrangements with the American company. There are no such stamp cancelling machines made in Canada, and I do not know there are any made in the world that are as good as these. I am afraid to say how many stamps this machine will cancel in a minute, but the letters pass through the machine so rapidly that no one can county them. It takes several men to feed the machine. A wheel revolving at a high rate of speed separates each letter from the rest to be carried to the obliterating stamp. The stamps are obliterated as the letters pass the lines. Hon. gentlemen will remember seeing the long bars extending three inches across the envelope in the vicinity of the stamp. These are lines made by the stamp cancelling machine.
$200 a year seems rather a large amount for the rental of a machine. '
They cannot be got any cheaper.
I was wondering whether these machines could be purchased.
No, they cannot be purchased.
Therefore you are obliged to rent them.
They are not obtainable in the United States or saleable there, and we could not manufacture them.
On what principle are the cotton duck bags used by the department kept in repair 1

The superintendent of stores branch, Mr. Sydney Smith, is in charge of that. I do not know what principle he adopts. He, I suppose, gives instructions throughout Canada that when bags get out of repair they should be returned to the stores to be dealt with. He has his officers and I suppose they overhaul the bags and have those repaired that require repairing. At one time there was a good deal of laxity in the matter of returning bags, and there was trouble between the department and the general public in seeing that bags were returned. Occasionally mail bags are sent out to private citizens. I dare say the hon. gentleman had occasionally had a mail bag delivered to him if he had a large amount of mail matter. The department is constantly endeavouring to get traces of these bags. Sometimes newspaper people get the bags and so on. The stores branch gather them in and overhaul them.

I must disclaim being of sufficient importance to have a mail bag devoted to myself. Therefore, I cannot be charged with the theft of mail bags. One can scarcely conceive that mail bags will be found in the same state of want of repair. Any one can very well understand that there [DOT] will be a large difference in the condition of the bags. There are the ordinary canvas bags for which the rate is 25 cents, and there are bags into which leather enters which cost more to repair. The department has fixed upon these figures as representing the fair average payment for repairs. The superintendent of that branch is Mr. Sydney Smith who is the eon of a former Postmaster General, and [DOT]who has been in the otfice for many years. On the 4th of May last, I asked a question relative to two mail services in the vicinity of the Manitoulin Islands. I asked if tenders has been called for them, and the Postmaster General replied yes. I have been informed that formerly the two services were in the one tender, that this year a man named Cleland tendered for $3,050 and that his tender was accepted on the first of April for the joint service, but afterwards he was informed by the department for reasons best known to themselves that the tender was at an end. This, after he placed himself in a position to undertake the duties, owning as he did a very valuable steamer. However the statement in the ' Hansard ' is that he had made a tender for what was afterwards put in two distinct tenders. May I ask the Postmaster General whether it is correct that this gentleman was asked to tender under an advertisement for what is now comprised in these two tenders 1 The reply in the ' Hansard ' is that for the service from Cutler to Wekinagong taking in the intermediate points of Spanish Mills and Little Current, was given, by contract to Simms Bros., at $1,500 per annum, and that the other service known as the Cutler and Gower Bay service was given to Herbert Cleland at $2,000, but he declined it unless he was given the other, and that the contract was given to Wm. Fraser at $1,800. These two services now cost $3,200. Is it correct that tenders were asked for these two services, or was one tender asked and was Mr. Cleland the lowest, and did the department decline to act on it ?

There is no foundation for the statement of the hon. gentleman for reasons best known to themselves. Speaking off hand, for I have not refreshed my memory with regard to that matter since that answer was made, the facts are as follows :	There had been
a service by boat from Cutler to Gore Bay, and I think to Kagawong, and on to the
terminal point of the route whatever that 'may be. I think the service extends from Cutler across to Gore Bay and thence to a terminal point which I suppose is Little Current. Whatever that terminal point is I desire the explanation to be considered to have reference to it. That service was performed by one vessel and the complaint was that it did not reach the terminal point at a sufficiently early hour. It had to leave Cutler on the arrival of the Canadian Pacific Railway train due at 4 p.m., and the distance was very considerable. The boat had only a speed of eight knots or eight miles an hour and this was considered unsatisfactory. The department decided to try to get a vessel of a greater speed, and if it could not get a vessel of sufficient speed to perform the service within a reasonable time so as to reach the terminal point iatl an early hour in the evening it would divide the service between two steamers, one going from Cutler to Kagawong, calling at Gore Bay, and the other going from Cutler to the terminal point. Accordingly, public tenders were invited. We asked for a steamer of twelve miles an hour. Tenders were put in. Mr. Cleland's I think, was one of the tenders, and so far as I remember, he only tendered for one of the services, that from Cutler to Gore Bay and Kagawong. He did not put in a separate tender for the other service ; but he accompanied his tender with a letter saying that he was prepared to perform the joint ser\ ice for a certain sum-I do not remember the amount. Is it stated in that letter ?

He wrote to the department saying that he was prepared to supply a vessel for the service, and the department telegraphed him that they would accept his offer. When the name of the vessel was mentioned, it was found to be the steamer which had performed the service before, the ' Telegram.' The department then communicated with him that if that was the vessel, it was known to have a speed of only eight miles an hour, and it would not be satisfactory. Mr. Cleland was invited to come to Ottawa to see if he could be arranged with to put on a steamer of proper speed. He came here, but no arrangement was made with him. It became necessary then to make other arrangements for the service. Accordingly, failing to get one vessel of sufficient speed to do the joint service, the department had to arrange to get separate *vessels to do the two services In the proper time. The result was that the two contracts *to which the hon. gentleman refers were *made. As to the price, I had not to do with the negotiations or the tenders, but my recollection is. though on this point I may be in error, that the price payable for the two services is less than the amount of Mr. COMMONS
Olelands' offer. Tlie only object of the department -was to get a good service, and we had either to get a faster vessel than the old one, or divide the service.
Are the two boats now performing the service capable of running twelve miles an hour ?
It is not necessary for the two to run twelve miles an hour, as they run on separate routes.
Did the advertisement for tenders say that the boats would have to be capable of running twelve knots an hour ?
The advertisement referred to the specifications and the proposed contract, which did name twelve miles an hour.

It would appear that in the preceding year there had been a contract for this service, and it was performed by the * Telegram ' for $3,400. Knowing that the contest would be keen this year, Mr. Cleland tendered at $3,050, and he was notified by the department that his tender would be accepted. The advertisement made no reference to the rate of speed required.

Will the hou. gentleman permit me ? I say that the advertisement notified the public where they would see the form of contract they were required to sign, and that form stated that the vessel would be required to have a speed of at least twelve miles an hour.

I am informed that there was nothing in the advertisement in regard to the rate of speed. The hon. Postmaster General states that it was referrable to the contract, which stated that it would be required to have a speed of twelve miles an hour, and included other details. When Mr. Cleland was informed that his was the lowest tender, he was notified to appear at Ottawa, and he did come down here. He assured the department that his boat would run twelve miles an hour, not including stops; but if stops were included, a boat would require to run eighteen miles an hour. The ' Telegram ' has always been considered a speedy boat, and I am informed that Mr. Cleland would have got the contract but for the interference with the department of the hon. member for Algoma.
There is not a word of truth in that.
When I asked the question about the contracts the hon. gentleman informed me that tenders were called for these two separate and distinct services. My information is that tenders were never !

called for these two separate and distinct services, but that tenders were asked for the total service, that Mr. Cleland was the lowest tenderer, and that he complied with the conditions, his vessel being capable of running twelve miles an hour, and he certainly attaches the blame to the hon. member for Algoma of having interfered with the department and prevented him getting tlie contract. When he came to Otawa he was told that although his boat did run twelve miles an hour, as required by the department, if the stoppages lessened her time he could not have the contract; and without any other tenders at all being called for, the contract was handed over to this man Simms, a most prominent partisan, a man who was mixed up with the Stratton matter in Ontario.

I think that the hon. gentleman is quite misinformed. The hon. member for Algoma in no way interfered. Mr. Cleland is a strong supporter of the present government, and we would have no reason politically for not giving him the contract. The only reason was that his vessel had not the speed required.
Were tenders called for these two services ?

That is my impression. The advertisement, I think, invited tenders in two ways-for one service' and a service divided into two parts. The form of contract brought me by the officer in charge asked for a vessel of twelve miles per hour, including stoppages. Mr. Clel-and's vessel had not that speed.

Mr. Cleland emphatically tells me that no tenders were called at all for the second service, and the only tender he ever made was for $3,050, and he guaranteed that his boat would run twelve miles an hour, but the department insisted that should include stoppages, which would mean eighteen miles per hour. He is emphatic in stating that the hon. member for Algoma interfered on behalf of Simms Bros, who are politicians of more than local repute and notoriety, and they got the patronage. Here is a letter from the Postmaster General which shows that Mr. Cleland felt he was harshly treated. He had a vessel worth $15,000 and had made a contract with the department when it was too late to put her on any other route for the season, and he was told that he could not have the contract, although his boat had the speed required. He went to one of the hon. gentleman's political friends. Mr. Williams, and Mr. Williams wrote protesting against the treatment. The reply was not that there had been public competition and that Mr. Cleland's tender was higher than the one accepted, but that the matter was urgent. Here is the reply :

Ottawa, April 20, 1903.
Dear Sir,-With farther reference to the mail service between Cutler and Manitowaning, since writing you on Saturday, the department has received offers for the performance of this service as two separate ones, and as the matter was urgent the offers have been accepted and instructions have been given to have the service established without delay. It will, therefore. not be possible for the department to make a contract with Captain Cleland as referred to in my letter of Saturday.
Yours sincerely,

D. Williams, Esq.,
The ' Collingwiood Bulletin,'
Collingwood, Ont.
It is evident that no tenders were called for. It was a case of unfair interference not to give the contract to this man when he was the lowest tenderer and guaranteed that his boat would run twelve miles an hour. Whether rightly or wrongly, Mr. Cleland blames the hon. member for Algoma for having interfered, and probably some day will be able to pay the lion, gentleman in kind.

I do not know that I can throw more light by further observations on the matter. Had the hon. gentleman intimated that he would bring this up, X would have refreshed my memory. The impression on my mind is that the advertisements were for one con tinuous service and also for a separate service of two parts. The hon. member for Algoma in no way interfered in regard to Mr. Cleland. He was anxious that the service should be equal to the requirements ; and from the papers submitted to me, I came to the conclusion that Mr. Cleland could not comply with the advertisement, and I do not think he pretended that his vessel had the speed required. He came to Ottawa within twenty-four hours after a telegram was sent to him, and the papers were submitted to me, and I learned that his vessel had not the proper speed.
Did he see the Postmaster General himself ?
No, he saw my deputy. I was not in Ottawa at the time.
Would the hon. gentleman bring down at the next sitting the names of those who tendered for the goods supplied by the Ottawa Supply Company ?
Yes, and the amount of each tender.
I asked the hon. gentleman the other evening if he knew where a mail clerk named Doyle came from and he said he did not. Has he found that out ?
I have not thought of it since.
Was there an appointment made recently of a mail clerk named Doyle ?
I cannot say, but I will get the information.

Can the hon. minister give any information as to the dismissal of the postmaster at the village of Port Lambton ? The post office was kept by a man named McNulty and was attended by Miss Ross, who was acting postmaster-probably deputy. The office was removed and Miss Ross was practically dismissed because of that removal. Perhaps the hon. minister cannot recollect
What county ?
In the disappearing riding of Bothwell, in the county of Lambton. I hope that the disclosure I have made of the locality will not give the hon. gentleman any pangs. Has he any recollection
No, I do not recollect.

I could hardly expect the hon. gentleman to be ready with the information without notice, I would ask him to bring down the correspondence and petitions presented to the department against the removal of the post office from the place where it was, and also against any action being taken on account of the displacement or dismissal of Miss Ross.

I will get that information. I understand the hon. gentleman to want all the correspondence and papers bearing upon the change of location and what he calls the dismissal of the postmaster, or leading to the former postmaster ceasing to be postmaster.
And the petitions.
Yes, I will see that all that information is given on the next item I have.
Would the hon. minister bring down the information as to why he dismissed the postmaster at Enterprise ?
I will get that as well.

Also the postmaster at Dead Creek.
